story-elements.text: Research suggests that our brains connect food with memory and emotions. However, I don’t think we need research as proof for this, because we all have experienced it. Whenever l eat or think of kadhi, it reminds me of my dadi ma. She would make the softest, smoothest kadhi pakora (we called it phulauri) I’ve ever tasted.

I remember those quiet afternoons when I would return home after school and sit cross-legged in the portico of my childhood home with a plateful of creamy kadhi-chawal, while dadi ma would sit beside me. Her kadhi had minimal spices, no onion or garlic, tempered with just cumin seeds, asafoetida, and dried red chillies. “The kadhi has to be stirred constantly so that the curd doesn’t curdle. That’s the rule,” she would say.

story-elements.title: Kadhi is typically eaten with rice.

story-elements.text: It was only when I moved to Delhi that I realised kadhi could have a different taste. One of my family friends from Uttarakhand shared a bowl of kadhi, and that was strikingly different from our Bihari phulauri. It had a lot of chopped onion and garlic, tempered with fenugreek, along with jeera and chillies, and was a little more tangy. And then I came across the kadhi chawal, served with onion slices and mint chutney combo from a famous roadside dhaba in Nehru Place. That too had a different flavour altogether.

Khaato from Rajasthan

According to culinary historians, kadhi likely originated in Rajasthan. Usha Dashora, a writer, filmmaker and traveller, who is from Rajasthan, told me that in earlier times, it was originally made from makki ka atta (corn flour). “Since there’s water scarcity in Rajasthan, people used buttermilk instead of water and then it became a tradition over time,” she explained. She also mentioned that even within the state, the taste of kadhi has evolved. In rural areas of Rajasthan, kadhi is thick and very tangy. The locals call it khaato, which is an altered version of khatta (sour). In the urban areas, it is much thinner and less sour, according to Usha.

K T Achaya, in his book Historical Dictionary of Indian Food, refers to themanam, a preparation mentioned in an older text, which is described as “resembling kadhi”. Another text speaks of a pulse-based kadhi, flavoured with asafoetida, an element still integral part of some modern kadhi recipes. These references indicate that such preparations have a long history in Indian cuisine.
Fajeto, the Gujarati version

Kadhi travels to Gujarat, evolving along the way. During summer, in Gujarat households, fajeto, the local version of kadhi, is often prepared alongside aamras. What makes fajeto distinct is that it is made using the residue left after extracting the mango pulp for aamras. The mango seed and skin are thoroughly washed in drinking water. And this water is then used to make kadhi, along with usual curd and besan. This lends the dish a slight sweetness and a distinct mango aroma. Typically made without garlic and onion, it’s a popular part of Jain meals in the summer.

story-elements.text:
Splash, that's a dubki kadhi
Arunima, a popular food vlogger, shared a distinct kadhi recipe from Chhattisgarh called dubki kadhi. Unlike other kadhi versions, it is made with urad dal instead of besan. The most interesting part is that the pakoras are not deep fried. Instead, small balls of the raw batter are gently dropped into the boiling kadhi where they take their little dubkis and simmer into the gravy until cooked to perfection.

Archana Pai Kulkarni, writer and former magazine editor, told me about the traditional Konkani Gaud Saraswati Brahmin (GSB) kadhi. This recipe specifically uses white pumpkin or bottle gourd (or sometimes okra) and fresh (not sour) buttermilk. Coconut is a must, and interestingly in some variations, a paste of raw rice is added besides the coconut paste, to enhance the thickness of the kadhi. Archana mentions two Konkani books — 500 Easy Recipes by Narayani Nayak and Ruchira by Kamalabai Ogle — for authentic cooking methods.
In the southern states

story-elements.title: South Indian versions use grated coconut, ginger, and assorted spices.

story-elements.text: From the north to the west, and the south of India, kadhi takes on unique forms. I was recently talking to my friend Namrata, founder of a literary consultancy and a food enthusiast, and was surprised to know that in Andhra Pradesh, her home state, there’s a chicken-based kadhi. The usual kadhi, called majjiga pulusu in Telugu (majjiga means buttermilk and pulusu is any spiced curry with gravy), also seems quite different from the Bihar and Delhi versions. It follows a sambhar style preparation where you add vegetables in the gravy, which varies with season. In summer, they add grated raw mango for flavour. In winters, bottlegourd, pumpkin, and drumsticks are common.

In Karnataka, the majjige huli uses a ground mix of grated coconut, dhaniya, jeera, green chillies, and black pepper, along with kadale bele (chana dal) or kadale hittu (besan), and yoghurt. Vegetables such as ash gourd, okra, and greens are also added. In majjiga pulusu too, the beaten curd is combined with a special paste made of coconut, green chillies, and coriander leaves. Tamil Nadu also uses a similar recipe.

Bhairav K, a culinary expert and manager at a three-star hotel in Delhi says, “Kadhi-chawal is one of the most popular dish combinations in India. An interesting blend of simplicity and richness, kadhi is widely loved for its tangy and spicy taste. When it’s tempered with ghee, asafoetida, curry leaves and dry red chillies, it becomes even more flavourful. Apart from its taste, it is preferred for its nutritional benefits as well.”

story-elements.title: Bhindi or okra is used in some versions.

story-elements.text: Kavita Devgan, a well known nutritionist, wellness consultant and author of Don’t Diet, says kadhi is not just tasty but also nutritious. It’s hydrating and has natural probiotic power. It delivers complete protein, as kadhi is made with besan and when combined with rice, the two together supply essential amino acids. The combination forms a better quality protein than either alone. It has a built-in anti-inflammatory mix as well.

story.headline: A taste of winter: Gajjak, Sandesh, Malaiyo & more
story.subheadline: Swatee Jog pens five traditional Indian winter delicacies that bring together seasonal ingredients, comforting flavours, and age-old culinary traditions

story-elements.text:
Here comes winter, long-awaited and much cherished. The season has its own culinary traditions and flavours. With the slightest dip in temperatures, Indian kitchens come alive with the aroma of nuts, jaggery and ghee. These recipes are rooted in the traditional practice of eating nutrient-rich ingredients that provide warmth and nourishment during the colder months. Here are six winter favourites you can recreate at home.

Gajjak
A winter staple in North India, particularly Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan, Gajjak is rich in flavour and wonderfully crisp. And yes, it is easy to make too!

Ingredients (Serves 4)
*1 cup white sesame seeds
*¾ cup grated jaggery
*1 tsp ghee
*¼ tsp cardamom powder

Method
*Dry-roast the sesame seeds over low heat until fragrant and they begin to pop. Keep aside.
*Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan. Add jaggery and 1 tbsp water, and melt over low heat.
*Cook until the syrup reaches the hard-crack stage. To test, drop a little syrup into cold water; it should turn brittle.
*Add the sesame seeds and cardamom powder. Mix quickly.
*Spread the mixture onto a greased plate or parchment paper and roll it out thinly while still warm.
*Cut into squares before it hardens completely.

Malaiyo 
Long before molecular gastronomy took over the world, India had its own cloud on a plate. Malaiyo is a seasonal speciality of Varanasi. Made from milk froth collected after leaving milk outdoors overnight in the winter chill, it has an extraordinarily light and airy texture.

Ingredients (Serves 4)
*1 litre full-fat milk
*½ cup fresh cream
*½ cup powdered sugar (adjust to taste)
*¼ tsp cardamom powder
*A few strands of saffron
*2 tbsp chopped pistachios and almonds

Method
*Boil the milk, simmer for 10 minutes and allow it to cool completely.
*Mix in the cream and transfer to a wide, shallow vessel.
*Traditionally, the milk is left overnight in the cool winter air, allowing a thick layer of cream and froth to form. For a home-friendly alternative, chill it thoroughly and use an electric whisk to whip the mixture until light and frothy.
*Add powdered sugar, cardamom powder and saffron.

Spoon the airy mixture into small bowls and garnish with chopped nuts.

Serve immediately while chilled.

Patisapta 
A much-loved delicacy during the Bengali harvest festival of Poush Parbon, Patisapta is a delicate, thin crepe filled with a sweet mixture of coconut, khoya and jaggery. Soft, mildly sweet and fragrant, it is a filling winter treat that brings families together.

Ingredients (Serves 4 – 8 crepes)

For the crepes:
*½ cup rice flour
*¼ cup all-purpose flour
*2 tbsp semolina
*1½ cups milk
*1 tbsp sugar

For the filling:
*1 cup grated coconut
*½ cup khoya
*½ cup grated jaggery
*¼ tsp cardamom powder

Method
*Mix rice flour, all-purpose flour, semolina, milk and sugar to make a smooth, thin batter. Allow it to rest for 20 minutes. Add a pinch of salt, if desired.
*In a pan, heat the grated coconut with jaggery and cook until the jaggery melts.
*Add khoya and cardamom powder. Stir until the mixture thickens.
*Heat a lightly greased non-stick pan. Pour in a ladleful of batter and spread it into a thin crepe.
*Cook until set. Place a spoonful of filling along one edge and roll gently.
*Cook for another minute and serve warm.

Nolen Gur Sandesh
Bengal's fragrant date palm jaggery, harvested during the colder months, comes alive when combined with fresh chenna (Indian cottage cheese). It transforms into Sandesh, a delicately sweet, melt-in-the-mouth dessert. Its distinctive caramel-like aroma and earthy sweetness make it one of Bengal's most treasured seasonal delicacies.

Ingredients (Serves 4 – 8 small pieces)
*2 cups fresh chenna (made by curdling approximately 1 litre of milk)
*½ cup grated Nolen Gur
*¼ tsp cardamom powder
*1 tsp ghee
*Chopped pistachios for garnish

Method
*Knead the fresh chenna gently until smooth and free of lumps.
*Heat a non-stick pan and add the chenna and grated Nolen Gur.
*Cook over low heat, stirring continuously, until the mixture thickens and comes together. Do not overcook, as it will turn rubbery.
*Add cardamom powder and allow the mixture to cool slightly.
*Shape into small round or oval portions, or press into traditional Sandesh moulds.
*Garnish with pistachios and chill briefly before serving.

Lapsi

A comforting dessert popular in Rajasthan and Gujarat, Lapsi is traditionally prepared during festivals, auspicious occasions and family celebrations. Its nutty flavour, soft, grainy texture and aroma of ghee make it particularly enjoyable during winter.

Ingredients (serves 4)
*1 cup coarse broken wheat (dalia)
*½ cup ghee
*¾ cup grated jaggery
*3 cups water
*¼ tsp cardamom powder
*2 tbsp chopped almonds and cashews
*1 tbsp raisins

Method
*Heat ghee in a heavy-bottomed pan. Add broken wheat and roast over low heat until golden brown and aromatic.
*Meanwhile, in a separate pan, dissolve jaggery in warm water and strain to remove impurities.
*Carefully add the jaggery water to the roasted wheat.
*Cover and cook over low heat for 20–25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the wheat softens and absorbs the liquid.
*Add cardamom powder, raisins and nuts. Mix well.
*Serve warm, garnished with a little extra ghee and chopped nuts.

story.headline: Karunadotsava | From ragi mudde to pandi curry, authentic dishes from Karnataka that every foodie must try
story.subheadline: As we celebrate Karnataka Rajyotsava this November, know about some of the cuisines of the State and try them out to celebrate the occasion.

story-elements.text:
What better way to celebrate a place than through its food? And when it comes to Karnataka, there is plenty to try and relish! From the humble ragi mudde and comforting bisi bele bath to soft sannas, neer dosa and spicy Coorgi pandi curry, every region has something special to offer.

This Karnataka Rajyotsava, let's take a foodie tour of the State and explore some of its authentic dishes that every foodie must taste.
Ragi mudde

Ragi mudde, or ragi ball, is a common food in central Karnataka. It is a part of homemade meals as well as restaurant menus, especially in districts such as Mandya, Mysuru, Bengaluru, Tumakuru and Hassan. Made with ragi (finger millet) flour and water, it is often paired with bean broths, vegetable sambar and meat gravies.

story-elements.text: Bisi bele bath

Bisi bele bath, which literally translates to “hot lentil rice” in Kannada, is a popular dish from Karnataka made with rice, lentils, vegetables and a blend of spices. Cooked together, these ingredients make for a flavourful, wholesome meal. It is best relished hot with a dollop of ghee, along with khara boondi or mixture.

story-elements.text: Sanna

Idli? No, wait. Sannas may look and even taste a bit like the much-loved South Indian breakfast staple, idli, but they are a popular delicacy in Mangaluru and surrounding regions. The dish is also widely prepared in Goa and the Konkan region of Maharashtra. Soft, spongy and slightly sweet, sannas are steamed rice cakes made from rice batter fermented traditionally using toddy or yeast. They can be eaten on their own or served with chutneys and other accompaniments.

story-elements.text: Neer dosa

Neer dosa is a much-loved delicacy from coastal Karnataka, especially the Tulu Nadu region. Made with a thin rice batter, these soft, light dosas are best enjoyed with a mix of grated coconut and jaggery, chutney or non-vegetarian gravies such as chicken curry.

story-elements.text: Patholi

Patholi is a traditional dish popular in coastal Karnataka. It is a stuffed rice flour dumpling steamed in turmeric leaf. Patholis are made in both sweet and spicy variations, with the sweet version being more popular and commonly prepared during festivals and celebrations. The sweet filling is made with freshly grated coconut and jaggery, flavoured with cardamom powder.

story-elements.text: Mandalu Oggarane

In Karnataka, they don't say, "Let's have chai and poha." Instead, they serve you some mandalu oggarane (also called mandakki oggarane) with mirchi bajji or onion pakodas. Mouthwatering, right? Made with seasoned puffed rice, mandalu oggarane is a popular breakfast dish and snack in the North Karnataka region.

story-elements.text: Ney kulu

Ney kulu is a traditional Kodava-style ghee rice. The aromatic, mildly flavored dish is known for its simple preparation and rich flavour. It is commonly served as part of lunch in Kodava homes. The aromatic rice is best enjoyed with with spicy gravies, rasam and bajjis.

story-elements.text: Pandi curry

Some travel to Kodagu to embrace nature, while several others ride there to taste the Kodava cuisine. One of the dishes from the region is pandi curry, prepared using tender pork and spices. Well, this gravy has a special sour ingredient called 'kachumpuli', an extract of a fruit grown locally. pandi curry is often served with rice, akki rotti or parota.

story-elements.text: Tambuli

Tambuli is one of the dishes that is perfect to beat the summer heat. It is a simple yoghurt-based preparation made with ingredients such as cucumber, herbs and leafy greens or raw mango, freshly grated coconut, spices and buttermilk. Neither a chutney nor a full-fledged gravy, tambuli has a taste of its own. This traditional dish from Malnad and coastal Karnataka is made with a variety of ingredients and served with rice.

story-elements.text: Kori rotti with kori gassi

For non-vegetarians, kori gassi is a must-try Mangalurean delicacy. This traditional chicken curry is prepared with coconut and a blend of spices. It is best enjoyed with kori rotti, thin and crispy rice wafers that are broken into pieces and soaked in the flavourful curry before eating.

story-elements.text: Jolada rotti with jhunka

Jolada rotti, made from jowar (sorghum) flour, is a popular and healthy alternative to regular chapatis and maida-based parottas in Karnataka and Maharashtra. A staple in North Karnataka homes, it is often served with a hot bowl of jhunka, a traditional dish made with gram flour (besan) and vegetables.

story-elements.text: Ennegayi

If you are not fond of brinjal, this dish might just change your mind. Ennegayi is a masala-rich and flavourful gravy made with brinjals, roasted peanuts, sesame seeds, coconut, onions, garlic, tamarind and a blend of spices. Popular across Karnataka, it tastes great with jolada rotti, chapatis and rice.

story-elements.text: Anjal masala fry

A trip to the beaches of Mangaluru or Udupi is incomplete without trying the local seafood. One such coastal delicacy is anjal masala fry, made with fresh kingfish (surmai) coated in a tangy, spicy marinade and fried until crisp on the outside while remaining tender and juicy on the inside. This dish is a treat for those who enjoy a good dose of spice.

story.subheadline: These iconic eateries offer a taste of the city’s enduring food traditions and also have a history that one can learn and be proud of.

story-elements.text:
If you’re in Karnataka’s capital city Bengaluru and want to explore the food that gives the city its distinct identity, skip the fancy restaurants for a day and follow the locals instead. For breakfast, start with a plate of soft idlis and chutney, move on to a crisp benne dosa, stop for a hot cup of filter coffee, and round off the day with a bun or puff from a traditional bakery. From bustling darshinis and iconic military hotels to old-school cafés, Bengaluru’s food story is best experienced one local favourite at a time. 

Here are some of the iconic eateries in Bengaluru that offer a taste of the city’s enduring food traditions and also have a history that one can learn and be proud of.

Darshinis and tiffin rooms that define breakfast

Darshinis in Bengaluru are more than affordable eateries. Their appeal lies in a simple formula: freshly prepared food, quick service, affordable prices and a hassle-free dining experience. The concept is often associated with the city's growth as a commercial and technology hub, where people needed convenient places to eat without spending too much time or money.

The format gained popularity in the 1980s, when 'Cafe Darshini' opened in Jayanagar and helped establish a model that spread across the city. 

Some of the iconic such eateries in the city include:

Vidyarthi Bhavan in Basavanagudi

Established in 1943, Vidyarthi Bhavan is among Bengaluru’s best-known breakfast places. Its crisp, golden masala dosas, served with chutney, have drawn generations of students and families to Gandhi Bazaar. 

Not just dosas, the outlet also serves rava idli, vada, khara bhath, kesari bhath, puri sagu and coffee.

Central Tiffin Room (CTR) in Malleshwaram

Better known as CTR Shri Sagar, this longstanding eatery has built its reputation on benne masala dosa — the generously buttered crisp dosa.

Mavalli Tiffin Rooms (MTR) on Lalbagh Road

Dating back to 1924, MTR is a landmark in the city's vegetarian dining tradition. Its menu features south Indian staples such as idli, dosa and bisi bele bath, but the restaurant is particularly known for rava idli, which was developed during wartime due to rice shortages. 

The outlet also serves a special thali, Chandrahara, a dessert, and fruit mixture.

Veena Stores in Malleshwaram

Started in 1977 as a small shop selling condiments and snacks, Veena Stores grew into one of Bengaluru’s most celebrated breakfast destinations. Its soft idlis, crisp vadas and distinctive green chutney have earned it a loyal following across generations. Shavige bath, khara bath and other traditional tiffin dishes round out the menu.

Sri Raghavendra Stores at Malleshwaram

Located near Malleshwaram railway station, Sri Raghavendra Stores is a favourite among commuters and breakfast seekers. Idli-vada, shavige bath, khara bath and chow chow bath are among its familiar offerings.

Brahmin’s Coffee Bar in Shankarapura

Operating since 1965, Brahmin’s Coffee Bar has earned a loyal following with its soft idlis, vadas, coconut chutney and filter coffee. The limited choice and stand-and-eat format are central to its identity. Its filter coffee is a favourite among regulars. The coffee is known for its strong, rich flavour and frothy finish.

Airlines Hotel on Lavelle Road

Airlines Hotel offers a different take on the traditional Bengaluru breakfast stop. Popular for South Indian tiffin and coffee, it has long been a place to meet friends, catch up over breakfast or take a break from the city's busy streets.

Some of the other hotels and darshinis you can visit include SLV Ragigudda, Upahara Darshini on DVG Road, Mudanna Hotel, Pai Hotel, Mudde Madappa Mess and Mahalakshmi Tiffin Room.

These establishments have survived changing tastes and generations of diners by sticking to uncomplicated menus. For many people, they are not just some places to eat, they are part of childhood memories.

Military hotels and the city's love for hearty meals

One can also find military hotels in Bengaluru. They are privately run eateries and are not to be mistaken for army canteens. Their precise origin remains debated, but their history is closely linked to the city's military communities and demand for filling, meat-based meals. Menus often include biryani, mutton chops, paya soup, keema and ragi mudde, with recipes passed down through families.

Unlike the lighter fare associated with the city's breakfast places, military hotels offer a distinctly different side of Bengaluru's culinary identity. Their appeal rests on generous portions, traditional cooking and dishes that have remained familiar over decades.

Shivaji Military Hotel in Jayanagar

Founded in 1935, a longstanding name in Bengaluru's non-vegetarian food scene, Shivaji Military Hotel is known for its Maratha-style cooking and donne biryani. The biryani is served in a bowl made from leaves, known as a donne, and is accompanied by dishes such as mutton fry and chicken. Chicken dry fry and donne biryani are their signature offerings.

Ranganna Military Hotel 

Starting as a small eatery in Domlur in 1964, Ranganna Military Hotel has grown into a familiar destination for traditional Karnataka non-vegetarian food. Its menu features paya, mutton curry served with dosa, mutton biryani, ragi mudde and bitter gourd curry. The establishment represents a style of cooking built around family recipes and freshly sourced meat.

Rajanna Military Hotel

A culinary tradition that began with just nine dishes has endured for decades at this modest Vijayanagar eatery. Rajanna, who hailed from Kunigal, drew on his experience working in a Bengaluru military hotel specialising in Maratha cuisine before setting up his own venture in a small shed 1985. Mutton features prominently on the menu here. The establishment has grown from being in a makeshift shed into a tiny eatery and is now run by Rajanna's wife and brother-in-law.

SG Rao's Military Hotel

Established in 1908 as 'Sri Govinda Rao Military Hotel', the eatery began serving Bengaluru’s first biryani at Akkipet. Its flavours reportedly won over even British soldiers. Its traditional non-vegetarian dishes and biryani later became favourites among wrestlers, or pailwans. In 2018, the eatery moved to Cottonpet and adopted the name SG Rao’s Military Hotel.

A go-to place for Andhra fare

Nagarjuna

The journey of this iconic restaurant began in 1984, when N Krishna Reddy, an agriculturist from Nellore in Andhra Pradesh, brought the region’s traditional cuisine to Bengaluru with the opening of a restaurant on Residency Road. It has both vegetarian and non-vegetarian food that gives traditional Andhra thali experience.

A quaint restaurant in the heart of the city

Koshy's on St Mark's Road

Since the 1940s, Koshy's has been a landmark of Bengaluru's café culture. Its menu spans familiar café fare, including cutlets, sandwiches, fish dishes and tea, reflecting the city's long-standing appetite for food influenced by multiple culinary traditions. Its old-world interiors and reputation as a meeting place have helped make it a favourite among generations of patrons, including artists, journalists and public figures.

Old-school bakeries and flavours of nostalgia

Traditional bakeries occupy a special place in the city's food culture. Their shelves bring together sweet and savoury favourites, from vegetable puffs and soft buns to honey cake, biscuits and rusks.

Albert Bakery in Frazer Town

Founded in 1902, Albert Bakery is a longstanding neighbourood favourite known for its old-world bakery character and savoury snacks. Its khova naan, keema samosas and bheja puffs make it a distinctive stop for those looking beyond the usual cakes and biscuits.

Thom's Bakery in Cox Town

Established in 1970 by P M Thomas as Thom's Cafe and Restaurant, Thom's Bakery is one of the city's familiar old-school baking places.

While the restaurant was shut after Thomas' passing, the bakery continues to be known for its everyday baked goods and festive plum cakes. It evokes a style of neighbourhood bakery where customers return for trusted favourites rather than elaborate presentations.

VB Bakery in VV Puram

Established in 1953, near Sajjan Rao Circle, VB Bakery is associated with the Congress bun (also known as the KBC or Khara Bun Congress), honey cake and other familiar bakery treats. Its appeal comes from the simple pleasures of Bengaluru's traditional bakeries: picking up a snack, carrying home a packet of baked goods or stopping for something sweet during an evening outing.

OG Variar and Sons in Rajajinagar

Variar Bakery is a popular stop for breads, rusks, biscuits, puffs and cakes. Its no-frills approach and familiar range of baked goods have earned it a steady following among residents. Like other old Bengaluru bakeries, it is as much a neighbourhood fixture as a place to pick up everyday snacks.

The many Iyengar bakeries

They are a defining feature of Bengaluru's streetscapes, found in almost every neighborhood across the city.

The Iyengar bakery tradition in Bengaluru can be traced back to 1898 when H S Thirumalachar opened the first-ever store (Bengaluru Brothers Bakery) in Chickpet. The bakeries are characterised by the aroma of freshly baked bread, biscuits, spicy puffs, and the warm glow of glass showcases.

Fatima Bakery and Supermarket 

The 60-year-old Fatima Bakery and Supermarket is located on Castle Street, Ashok Nagar. It was relocated in 2017 after its original place was demolished to make way for Namma Metro. In 1957, V P Francis and his younger brother from Kerala set up the bakery. It is known for its savoury puffs, rolls, breads and cakes. Its popular picks include chicken puffs, lemon and almond rolls, chocolate sponge cake and coconut biscuits. The bakery is also associated with festive favourites such as plum cake.
Together, these eateries tell the story of a city shaped by generations. Exploring these local favourites is a way to experience Bengaluru beyond its IT corridors.

story-elements.text: 1. Cheenikayi kadubu

This delicacy from Malnad and coastal Karnataka is made with grated cheenikayi (sweet yellow pumpkin), broken rice or rava (semolina), and jaggery, wrapped in plantain leaves and steamed. This sweet is often made for Deepavali.
2. Mudalur muscoth halwa

Muscoth, spelt musket or muscat, is coconut milk in Sinhalese. The halwa is made of coconut milk, wheat (or all-purpose) flour, milk extracted from the flour, sugar or jaggery. The jelly-like sweet has been made popular in Tamil Nadu’s Mudalur and has a geographical indication (GI) tag as well. The book, Homestyle Southeast Asian Cooking by Rani King and Chandra Khan, the Sri Lanka muscat as similar to the very fragrant Turkish delight but “far superior”.

3. Pootharekhulu

This GI-tagged sweet is said to have originated from Atreyapuram in Andhra Pradesh. It is made of paper-thin rice crepes that are stuffed with jaggery, ghee and dry fruits, and rolled. Pootha means coating and rekhulu refers to the sheets made from fermented rice batter spread very lightly on a griddle.

linked-story.headline: Mithai, minus the guilt this Deepavali

story-elements.text: Mithai, minus the guilt this Deepavali
4. Sukrunde

This easy-to-make sweet is crispy on the outside with a soft filling, and is popular in coastal Karnataka, Konkan, and Goa regions. The stuffing is made of cooked dals (usually chana dal), grated coconut, and jaggery, while the batter is made of rice flour and besan. Rasachandrika, a famous Marathi compendium of  Saraswat cooking, also includes a recipe of sukrunde made of boiled green gram.
5. Kervai

This sweet comes from Parsi culinary heritage. Ripe banana is mashed and stuffed with dry fruits and nuts, and coated with a rice flour paste and fried. It finds mention in A Gourmet’s Handbook of Parsi Cuisine by the late Bapsi Nariman, author of cookbooks.

headline: Partition, food & Memory: Echoes from an undivided kitchen

seo.meta-description: Bengali cuisine history: How displacement, the Bangal-Ghoti divide and refugee resettlement shaped food traditions across India after 1947.
seo.meta-title: Partition food: Echoes from an undivided kitchen & culinary heritage

story.headline: Partition, food & Memory: Echoes from an undivided kitchen
story.subheadline: When refugees arrived in Calcutta, food was not the first thing on their minds. Many had fled with whatever little they could carry, leaving behind familiar ways of life.
story.custom-slug: Partition, food & Memory: Echoes from an undivided kitchen

story-elements.text: In ‘Abar Ashibo Phire’ (‘I Shall Return’), poet Jibanananda Das imagined returning to the rivers, fields, and landscapes of rural Bengal — as a bird drifting across the sky, as a spotted owl hooting on a silk cotton tree, a child spilling puffed rice to feed the fowls, or as a young man wading through the muddy waters.

Written in 1934, before Partition, the poem evokes associations of an undivided Bengal and its intimate relationship with nature. Published much later, in 1957, when Bengal’s reality had changed completely, the poem’s longing for a familiar landscape acquired a different resonance for Bengalis. For those who migrated from East Bengal, the loss extended beyond their homes and land to the rivers, ponds, fields, and kitchens that shaped their food traditions.

When refugees arrived in Calcutta, food was not the first thing on their minds. Many had fled with whatever little they could carry, leaving behind familiar ways of life. At Sealdah station, they registered themselves as refugees before being directed to camps and settlements across the country. Their previous occupations and backgrounds partly determined where they were sent to — primarily rural Bengal, Odisha, Dandakaaranya (forested regions of east and central India), Madhya Pradesh, and the Andaman Islands.

It’s important to understand food histories of Partition through displacement and survival, anthropologist Amrita Bhattacharya points out. “In many colonies, financial constraints changed what families could afford to eat. Depending on how much money they had, they served their children only a small fish or half an egg,” she notes.

story-elements.title: Kochur loti diye chingri (prawns with taro stolons)
Gima shaak er bora (Indian chickweed fritters)
Aloo r kosha bhaja (fried potato skin)

story-elements.text: Bangal-Ghoti divide

Partition created a divide within Bengali society that continues to shape how people identify themselves. Those who migrated from East Bengal came to be known as Bangals, while the people of West Bengal were identified as Ghotis.

Bangal cooking is often associated with the pungency of mustard paste, while Ghoti preparations are known for their use of posto (poppy seeds). Culinary enthusiast Pritha Dutta points out that the differences between the two food cultures became a source of affectionate rivalry. “The rivalry could even find its way to the dining table: was mustard the answer to everything, or could posto make a dish just as memorable?” Pritha jokes. The divide also carries the unresolved social and political tensions of Partition. Amit Sen, Amrita’s partner, also an anthropologist, describes the uncomfortable perception that refugees “usurped” and “grabbed” land from the local communities, adding that the historical context of refugee resettlement complicates this idea.

Yet, the distinction between Bangal and Ghoti food is not as clear-cut as popular perceptions suggest. One common misconception, Amrita points out, is that dried fish is exclusive to Bangal cuisine. But Ghoti communities in many parts of Bengal also eat dried fish, albeit prepared in their own way, she adds. “Along the banks of the river in Birbhum and Bardman, there were many East Bengali communities who were given land. Even today, if you travel there, you can at once see that the kind of vegetables grown and farming practices are very different. The local people do not practise the same kind of organised farming,” says Amit.

He also makes a larger observation about refugees in Dandakaaranya and Madhya Pradesh — “Bengali settlers contributed to the expansion of rice cultivation in areas where millets were traditionally the staple of the indigenous (Adivasi) communities. It’s not only that the refugees changed their own food habits. They also affected the food habits of the locals,” she says.

Refugees who were sent to the Andaman Islands had to negotiate a different landscape and food ecology. For people accustomed to freshwater fish, particularly hilsa (ilish), the shift to an island environment meant adapting to unfamiliar sources of food. Amrita observes that they turned to fish such as mullet, catfish, and koi macchi, found in the mangrove brackish creeks, and incorporated local ingredients such as tapioca, cassava and taro root.

She also mentions a wild green dheki shaak, an edible fern which grew in abundance near damp areas, canal banks, and ponds. The refugees in the Andamans, looking for familiar ingredients, encountered a different variety, the mangrove fern, growing near the sea. Because this fern absorbs coastal minerals, it is naturally salty and does not require additional salt while cooking.

Bengalis living in the Andamans were also influenced by the cooking styles of the local Tamil fishing community, the Sri Lankans, and communities from Jharkhand who were referred to as ‘Ranchi-wala’. “Primarily, they used to have rice three times a day but shifted to bread and chapati. They replaced their usual catla and rohu fish with kokari mach and sardines,” she adds.
What was lost?

“The preparations most vulnerable to being lost were also the least likely to find their way into cook books,” says Pritha. She recalls dishes such as holud patar dal (lentils scented with fresh turmeric leaves), chapor ghonto (lentil cakes cooked with seasonal vegetables) and mulor ambal (a sweet-and-sour radish preparation). “There were also countless ways of using vegetable skins, stalks and leaves, including knachkolar khosa bata, made with raw banana peel.”

Kochur loti (taro stolons) cooked with prawns, the pungent flavours of shutki (dried fish associated with particular regional food cultures of Chittagong and Barishal), small fish such as amodi and loittya, water-lily stems known as shapla, and greens such as paatshaak and kochushaak were used in everyday cooking in parts of East Bengal.

These ingredients were not always easy to find in Calcutta, and even when substitutes were available, they could not quite recreate the familiar taste. Pritha recalls her friend mentioning how Bangladeshi-British chefs brought satkora, an aromatic citrus fruit integral to Sylheti fish and meat curries, back into the spotlight at a Kolkata food festival.

“Seasonal sweets and pithe-puli marked the Bengali winter, with preparations using date-palm jaggery, coconut, and newly harvested rice. Others, such as narkele chira, involved painstakingly shaving coconut with a traditional tool called a norun, before coating it in sugar syrup and drying it,” she adds, saying making pithas was also a collective activity, with the process itself becoming a way of preserving rituals and memories of home.

The food of East Bengal did not disappear completely with Partition. It travelled with the people who left, changed with the landscapes they settled in and survived in memories and kitchens. Some recipes endured, others adapted, and many were gradually forgotten. Today, both the bold-pungent ilish bhapa and the milder-richer chingri malaikari have become integral to a Bengali thali.

headline: Let the good times fizz! Four easy-to-make mocktails to liven up your festive parties

seo.meta-title: Mocktail recipes: Four easy drinks to liven up your festive parties

story.subheadline: Swatee Jog shares four easy-to-make mocktail recipes featuring jamun, mango, blueberry and green apple to keep your celebrations bubbling with flavour.

story-elements.text:
The festive season gives you the perfect reason to host sundowner parties with family and friends. The menu may be elaborate, with Indian dinner staples piling up on the table. But your mocktails can bring a refreshing burst of flavour and colour.

A perfect mocktail balances four elements: sweetness, acidity, aroma, and fizz. Fruit purees lend body, a dash of citrus adds contrast, herbs and spices bring complexity, and soda provides that celebratory sparkle. Floral notes such as rose and hibiscus add elegance, while ingredients such as ginger, black pepper, and cardamom keep the drinks from becoming cloyingly sweet.

Here are a few festive recipes. Serve them in wine glasses, coupe glasses, tall tumblers, or traditional brass glasses for a festive touch.

Jamun, Rosemary and Lime Blast

Jamun makes for a dramatic-looking mocktail, while rosemary contributes a woody, pine-like aroma that contrasts beautifully with the fruit’s natural tartness. Lime and soda keep everything lively.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 2 cups ripe jamun, deseeded and pureed, or 1 cup canned jamun juice

— 60 ml fresh lime juice

— 60 ml sugar syrup, or to taste

— 4 small sprigs of fresh rosemary

— 600 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— Thin lime wheels, for garnish

— 4 small rosemary sprigs, for serving

Method

— Blend the jamun puree with the lime juice and sugar syrup until smooth.

— Lightly bruise four small rosemary sprigs between your fingers to release their aroma. Add them to the jamun mixture and leave to infuse for five minutes. Remove the sprigs.

— Divide the mixture equally among four ice-filled glasses.

— Top each glass with approximately 150 ml of chilled soda and stir gently.

— Garnish with a lime wheel and a fresh rosemary sprig.

linked-story.headline: High on sobriety

story-elements.text: High on sobriety

Blueberry, Orange Blossom and Vanilla Fizz

This feels almost like a dessert in a glass. Blueberries bring dark-fruit notes, orange blossom water lends a delicate floral aroma, and vanilla rounds out the sharper flavours.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 250 g blueberries, fresh or frozen

— 400 ml chilled water

— 80 ml fresh orange juice

— 40 ml fresh lemon juice

— 60 ml sugar syrup

— 2–4 drops of food-grade orange blossom water

— ¼ tsp vanilla extract

— 400 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— Orange peel twists, for garnish

Method

— Place the blueberries in a saucepan with 100 ml of water. Simmer gently for five minutes, pressing the berries lightly to release their juice.

— Cool the mixture and strain it through a fine sieve, pressing gently to extract the liquid. Allow it to cool completely.

— Combine the blueberry liquid with the remaining water, orange juice, lemon juice and sugar syrup.

— Add the vanilla extract and two drops of orange blossom water. Stir, taste and add another drop or two only if needed.

— Fill four glasses with ice and divide the blueberry mixture equally.

— Top each glass with approximately 100 ml of soda.

— Twist a strip of orange peel over each glass to release its fragrant oils, then use it as a garnish.

Mango, Passion Fruit, Saffron and Lime Cooler

Mango and passion fruit come together for a satisfying contrast: mango provides luscious sweetness, while passion fruit contributes acidity and a distinctive fragrance. Saffron adds subtle floral warmth that makes this drink especially suited to festive occasions.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 300 ml mango pulp or thick mango juice

— 150 ml passion fruit pulp or juice

— 50 ml fresh lime juice

— 1 generous pinch of saffron strands

— 2 tbsp warm water

— 30–45 ml sugar syrup, optional

— 400 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— 4 small mint sprigs, for garnish

— A few passion fruit seeds, for garnish

Method

— Place the saffron strands in two tablespoons of warm water and leave to infuse for 10–15 minutes.

— In a jug, combine the mango pulp, passion fruit pulp and lime juice.

— Add the saffron infusion, including the strands if desired, and mix well.

— Taste before adding sugar syrup. Adjust the consistency with a little water if required.

— Fill four glasses with ice and divide the fruit mixture equally.

— Top each glass with approximately 100 ml of soda, stirring gently to combine.

— Garnish with mint and a few passion fruit seeds.

linked-story.headline: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

story-elements.text: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

Green Apple, Cucumber, Mint and Chilli Refresh

This refreshing combination is ideal for guests who prefer something sharper and less sugary. Green apple gives the drink a tart backbone, cucumber keeps it fresh, mint adds fragrance, and chilli supplies a restrained burst of heat.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 400 ml green apple juice

— 150 g cucumber, peeled and chopped

— 40 ml fresh lime juice

— 15–20 mint leaves

— 1 small green chilli, deseeded

— 30–45 ml sugar syrup, optional

— 500 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— 4 cucumber ribbons

— 4 small mint sprigs, for garnish

Method

— Blend the cucumber with 100 ml of the apple juice until smooth.

— Strain through a fine sieve into a jug.

— Add the remaining apple juice, lime juice and mint leaves.

— Slice the deseeded chilli very thinly. Add one or two slices to the jug, stir and taste after two minutes. Remove them once the desired level of heat is achieved.

— Add sugar syrup if needed, especially if the apple juice is particularly tart.

— Divide the mixture between four ice-filled glasses.

— Top each with approximately 125 ml of soda and stir gently.

— Garnish with a cucumber ribbon and a mint sprig.

f77885ca-7b89-4c01-a616-81d92613e2e6.headline: Mithai, minus the guilt this Deepavali

story.subheadline: Tini Sara Anien shares simple ways to enjoy Deepavali treats without the guilt

story-elements.text:
Deepavali is here, and the mithai temptation is hard to resist. Laddoos, chaklis, kaju katlis, and Amma's familiar "Just taste this one" can quickly add up to a feast. But you don't have to give up the festive treats to eat sensibly. You just have to eat like you actually mean it.

Try the three-bite rule

Want to taste everything? You can, just don't consume the entire sweet.

"Cut them into bite-sized pieces rather than taking whole portions," says dietician Sakshi Jain. "If the platter has Mysore pak, badam halwa, kaju katli, and coconut barfi, take a little of each. You get all the flavours without eating too much of any one sweet," she adds.

Eat slowly and actually taste it. The ghee, the crunch, the melt. Also, identifying your favourite sweets always helps narrow down the choices.

linked-story.headline: Mithai, minus the guilt this Deepavali

story-elements.text: Mithai, minus the guilt this Deepavali

Make sharing a tradition

Don't open five boxes and work through them alone for the next week. Nutritionist Kanika S suggests creating a tasting platter.

"Cut larger mithai into smaller portions and arrange them alongside savoury favourites like kodubale, nippattu, ribbon pakoda, and chakli. Everyone can sample different varieties without having to eat the entire sweet," she explains. Or swap with neighbours. You send your adhirasam, they send their murukku.

Don't skip your meals

If you skip a meal and arrive at dinner hungry, "you could eat the tablecloth".

"This often leads to one eating twice as much and feeling terrible after. Stick to your timings. Have a proper breakfast. If you know lunch is going to be grand, just make breakfast a little lighter," says Kanika. Don't skip a meal altogether.

Add colour to your plate

Your plate doesn't have to be just brown, fried, and glistening with ghee. Add a pop of green, orange, red, and yellow.

"Pair your vegetable pulao or bisibele bath with cucumber kosambari, beans palya, or a bowl of sundal. Throw in some sprouts chaat, roasted chana, or steamed corn," dietician Tanishk Rao says. Such dishes balance out the heavy stuff and give you enough fibre.

linked-story.headline: This Deepavali, make it about less scrolling, more bonding

story-elements.text: This Deepavali, make it about less scrolling, more bonding

Sip smart

One glass of aerated drink, one sweetened juice, one "just one more", and you end up consuming the sugar equivalent of three laddoos without noticing.

"Choose buttermilk, lemon juice with less sugar, tender coconut water, or water infused with mint and cucumber. Homemade jaljeera or a lightly sweetened aam panna works too," says Tanishk. You'll stay hydrated, feel lighter, and still have something fun to sip in your glass.

Make movement part of the party

You don't need a gym session on Deepavali day.

"You just need to move a little. Go for a slow post-meal walk with the family. Put on some music and dance in the living room with friends. Get everyone to help with the lights and decorations. Play badminton. Play catch with the kids. None of these activities will feel like exercise," lists out Sakshi.

story.subheadline: Some scientists at the ICAR-CPRI (Indian Council of Agricultural Research- Central Potato Research Institute) have developed nutrient-rich potato varieties, namely ‘Kufri neelkanth’, ‘Kufri manik’, and ‘Kufri jamunia’, bioengineered forms aimed at improving nutritional deficiencies.

story-elements.text:
India is the second largest producer of potatoes in the world after China, the Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences have said.

It won’t be an exaggeration to call the tuberous root as one of the most reliable food sources in Indian kitchens.

There are some considerable reasons for it being a popular addition to Indian food dishes — it has versatility of taking on any flavor, is economical for frequent consumption and can provide nutritive sustenance.

The average cost of potato in the Indian market ranges between rupees 20 to rupees 35 per kilogram, whether one purchases from a wholesale mandi (even less), a market or an online store.

While potatoes have earned some bad names for containing excessive calories, enabling the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) and National Institute of Nutrition (NIN) to often remain silent on its consumption by adults, the vegetable is not inherently bad for health, others have argued.

As per experts, the way potato is treated in a kitchen, used or consumed decides how nutritious it can be for people.

While boiled or mashed potatoes consumed in moderation can be nutritious, deep frying them in rich oil or having fries can make them an unhealthy choice.

linked-story.headline: Sweet Potato Masala Chapati Recipe | A delicious twist to your everyday Chapati!

story-elements.text: Sweet Potato Masala Chapati Recipe | A delicious twist to your everyday Chapati!

Biofortified potato in India

With India battling hidden hunger, arising from nutritional deficiencies in people, and its dependency on potato to be a side dish or even the main meal on other days, scientists are eyeing it to become a biofortified crop, ensuring enhanced nutrition and accessibility.

Some scientists at the ICAR-CPRI (Indian Council of Agricultural Research- Central Potato Research Institute) have developed nutrient-rich potato varieties, namely ‘Kufri neelkanth’, ‘Kufri manik’, and ‘Kufri jamunia’. 

Promoted by the central government, ‘Kufri jamunia’, a purple skinned potato has become the most advanced form of the vegetable due to higher levels of Vitamin C, anthocyanins, and carotenoids present in them, making its nutritional profile richer than the white or brown fleshed forms.

Biofortified crops have been grown to solve hunger or hidden deficiency.

Nutritional deficiencies among Indians is not limited to just undernourished people but also to those who are taking in adequate calories but not sufficient micronutrients.

Iron, folate, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D and others are some most commonly missed micronutrients in food.

If remained untreated, they can turn into anemia, pregnancy complications, psychiatric or neurological troubles over time.

As per scientists, biofortified crops can be a solution to this problem.

Biofortification involves directly embedding the essential nutrients directly into the crops while they are growing out from the soil, the World Health Organization (WHO) has stated.

Being densely packed with micronutrients, biofortified crops can cover up for vitamin and mineral loss.

Colored potatoes for a reason

Growing biofortification research has highlighted the development of colored fruits and vegetables.

This change is not random but backed up by science.

The natural pigments, such as anthocyanins and carotenoids, which give them colors also make them rich with antioxidants.

Antioxidants nullify the effects of free radicals in the body, charged molecules contributing to systemic inflammation in the body.

They are also rich in iron and zinc.

‘Kufri jamunia’

Officially released in 2024, ‘Kufri jamunia’ has higher levels of ascorbic acid, anthocyanin, and carotenoids than ‘Kufri manik’ and ‘Kufri neelkanth’, the two previous biofortified varieties.

Apart from being rich in iron, zinc, vitamins and other minerals, this variety is also observed to have a rich consumer appeal.

As per records, the purple skinned potato contains 42.75 mg of Vitamin C per 100 grams of flesh as compared to 23.15 mg of the same in a normal white potato.

The variety has also shown growth in multi location trials, however, has been recommended for North Indian soil.

What about the cost?

While biofortification essentially means to improve micronutrient content through crop breeding, it does not add any further strain on the agriculture process.

As per reports, these crops don’t require to be treated with any additional biofertilizers or any other form of specialized treatment.

Hence, some scientists call them cost effective.

Many studies have also stated that biofortification can be a good step ahead to ensure better nutrition at affordable food cost.

headline: Karunadotsava | Think you know Karnataka food? These chefs are serving up flavours you've probably never tried

seo.meta-description: Regional dishes: Chefs, home cooks and researchers across Karnataka are serving lesser known micro-cuisines through pop-ups, curated dinners and cafes.
seo.meta-title: Karnataka food: Chefs and home cooks preserve lesser known micro-cuisines

story.headline: Karunadotsava | Think you know Karnataka food? These chefs are serving up flavours you've probably never tried
story.subheadline: From Malnad's kobbari neer pundi to the Beary community's thulcha poothala, many home chefs are preserving lesser known micro-cuisines of Karnataka in varied formats.
story.custom-slug: KArunadotsava | Think you know Karnataka food? These chefs are serving up flavours you've probably never tried

story-elements.text: “I was unwell one day and wanted to order appehuli (a tangy raw mango preparation from coastal Karnataka and the Malnad region),” says Bengaluru-based Dr Darshan Gowda, Founder of Dakshin Soirée, an experiential dining enterprise rooted in South Indian food traditions. It was nowhere to be found on delivery platforms, in a city where Greek, Vietnamese, and Turkish food are a few taps away.

Many Kannadigas will recognise that moment. The food that fills our homes, from weekday saaru to wedding spreads, has rarely made it onto restaurant menus, let alone delivery apps. That is changing. Across the state, chefs, home cooks and researchers are now carrying it to new tables: curated dinners, a home dining room, a travelling supper club, a Karnataka-forward cafe and five-star pop-ups. Between them, they are making the case for Karnataka’s many micro-cuisines. For anyone who knows the state only through idli or dosae, it is an invitation to look again.

story-elements.title: Ole Project: Ole Project’s Malnad pudina raw jackfruit wrapped in pandan leaves (biriyani soppu) with hunase hasi gojju chimichurri (tamarind sauce ).

story-elements.text: Looking again is what Dr Darshan’s menus ask of diners. Dakshin Soirée, which he started about three years ago, hosts a new multi-course experience roughly every 45 days. ‘Communities of Karavali’ travelled down the coast, from yetti tisre chutney (dry shrimp and clams) in Mangaluru and punarpuli meen (fish with kokum, steamed in banana leaf) in Karwar to Bhatkali biryani.

Beegara Oota (a non-vegetarian feast for relatives by marriage) turned inland, with onameen uppinkaayi, a sun-cured dry fish pickle from Chamarajanagar. For Rajyotsava, his Malnad Maduve Oota (a Malnad wedding feast) brings jeegujje podi (breadfruit in a red chilli crust) and kobbari neer pundi, coconut-stuffed rice dumplings simmered in coconut milk. Read together, the menus work almost like a map of the state. A region, Dr Darshan believes, is far more than the few dishes that have come to stand for it. “There are many communities, ingredients, cooking techniques and food traditions that deserve the same attention,” he says.
Putting the Bearys on the map
Among those communities are the Bearys of Mangaluru, “well-known within our community, but almost strangers to outsiders”, says Nazeera Mohidine, a Beary food documentarian.

story-elements.title: Beary dishes are not often documented and archived

story-elements.text: The name, she explains, comes from the Tulu vyapari (trader) and the Arabic bahar (sea), and that trading history lives on in the food. Beary cooking is mildly spiced, leans on badesaunf (fennel) over jeera (cumin), and has dishes like thulcha poothala, which she says is almost dying. Ground rice and egg are beaten into a foam, cooked like a dosa and filled with coconut, sugar and chana dal.

Searching online for the recipes she grew up with, she found only a scattered few, none written by Bearys. Since 2020, she has documented 50 recipes on Instagram. In October, with Coastal Collective Heritage, she opened her home for Daawath’g Baru (come for the feast, in Beary), where guests were taught to make mass ro unde, rice balls stuffed with coconut, red chilli paste and mass (dried tuna). “Mass carries the history of our trade with Lakshadweep on its back,” she says, adding that she hopes to have many such tables, “to put Beary food on the world map”. Young Bearys settled abroad write to tell her that online recipes help them cook home food away from home.
Archiving Karnataka

Away from home is also where Anusha Venkatesh, founder and culinary curator at Ole Project, realised how much she had taken her food for granted. In Canada, she found avarekai (hyacinth beans) in a frozen aisle, cooked uppittu (savoury semolina dish) with it, and cried. With almost nowhere to eat the food she grew up on, she started calling aunties back home for the recipes no restaurant made. Ole Project took shape in 2022 and now documents food across the state’s four broad regions. Since September 2024, it has also been a travelling kitchen. Its Jawari (North Karnataka cuisine) menu changes the format, never the recipe: kadak jowar rotti becomes nachos and chutney becomes salsa. A classic ragi mudde, Anusha says, can feel exclusionary to anyone who does not know how to eat it. “I will source the ragi and make the ragi mudde, but I might not present it as a ragi mudde to you,” she says. Seventy per cent of the guests at Ole’s North Karnataka pop-up were from the region, people who eat these flavours every day.
Beyond fine dining

Everyday tables are where Chef Shriya Shetty, Founder – BuCo. artisanal bakery and cafe, wants this food. Working at a modern Indian restaurant abroad, she realised she had no clue how to cook Indian food, and felt embarrassed about it. So she set out to study the food of Mangaluru, where her roots are. Her pop-ups were built to show that Mangalurean food is more than ghee roast, neer dosa and kori rotti. Four years ago, BuCo became a Karnataka-forward cafe, her favourite format. “I don’t want the emergence of regional cuisines to only be fine dine, we need to inculcate it into every aspect of F&B,” she says.

She has a point; this was always everyday food. She uses the most basic ingredients, red amaranth, ridge gourd, dry fish, and lets technique and pairing show what they can do. Her Instagram series, Taste Against Time, features everyday food with indigenous ingredients, because recipes keep evolving, she says, but lose the ingredients and you lose the cuisine.
Bannur mutton goes premium

One ingredient sits at the heart of Chef Kalyan Gopalakrishna’s cooking: Bannur mutton, which his family has used for about 150 years. His Karnivore Kitchen, a delivery-only kitchen in North Bengaluru, serves Old Bengaluru Naati cuisine, naati meaning hyperlocal in Kannada, Telugu and Tamil. Think kothmiri bannur mutton fry or naati koli saaru. Talking to friends in the industry, he realised most people did not think Karnataka food was worthy of fine dining. So he positioned Old Bengaluru Naati food as premium and took it into pre-plated pop-ups at five-star hotels.

For spirit-paired dinners, food meant to be eaten by hand had to be plated for cutlery. “The taste and the flavours would never change. It is just the form and the plating that we work around with,” he says. Karnataka, he adds, has 10 to 12 distinct cuisines, and he showcases them every chance he gets.
Making the interest last

Showcasing is a start; staying power is the real test. Gowda does not believe Karnataka’s food needs to go viral or win Western validation to be valued. “Regional cuisine should not become another trend that disappears when something new comes along,” he says. More than a trend, these efforts feel like a homecoming, with recipes once kept in kitchens and memories now written down, plated and passed around. This Rajyotsava, there is plenty on Karnataka’s table to be proud of.

headline: Steamed to perfection: The secret behind Palakkad's famous Ramassery idli

seo.meta-description: Kerala food: Journey to Palakkad village to taste soft Ramassery idlis. Traditional recipe, wood fire steaming method, and local heritage from Mudaliar weavers explained.
seo.meta-title: Ramassery Idlis: Unravelling the secrets of Kerala village special delicacy

story.headline: Steamed to perfection: The secret behind Palakkad's famous Ramassery idli
story.subheadline: The selection of rice is very important in making Ramassery idlis. The taste depends on the boiling of paddy.

story-elements.text: After a customary visit to Palakkad, I set off on a culinary sojourn to the nondescript village of Ramassery in the same district to savour the dosa-like idlis there. I headed to the Saraswathi Tea Stall to have a taste of these special idlis. Akin to thatte idlis of Karnataka, they are flat, circular, and similar to a dosa in shape. These soft, fluffy idlis leave one craving for more. The steamed delicacies melt in your mouth and make sure that you don’t stop at one. But for these idlis, this tiny hamlet sans religious or historical attractions would have remained in obscurity on the tourist map of Kerala. The genesis of these idlis can be traced back to the Mudaliar community of weavers who migrated from Tamil Nadu and settled down in Ramassery. Earlier, they were known to pay idlis as wages to the labourers who helped with weaving. When the weaving business was in dire straits, the women had to shift to making idlis; the men would go around peddling them. The family that currently runs Saraswathi Tea Stall converted a portion of their house into a small shop for selling idlis. As more people began to buy the idlis, a tea stall was set up.
Subsequently, when the family grew larger, more eateries sprung up. There are several such stalls, each one making over 2,000 idlis per day.
Variety of rice matters

linked-story.headline: Durban dish, desi twist

story-elements.text: Durban dish, desi twist

The selection of rice is very important in making Ramassery idlis. The taste depends on the boiling of paddy. The combination of rice and black gram is equally important as the drying and de-husking, which needs to be done in a particular way. The recipe remains a trade secret. Though made of rice and split pea lentils, just like idlis, the proportion of the cereals and the consistency of the batter are different. Earlier, the idlis were steam-cooked in unglazed earthen pots arranged in a three-tiered manner only in the searing heat of a wood stove using the tamarind tree wood. Women would sit hunched over a wood fired stove in a smoky kitchen, sweat it out in front of the fire and churn out 100 idlis an hour. Three eight-inch round clay containers are covered with pieces of wet cotton cloth. A ladle full of batter is poured on each of the prepared clay steamer containers.
These are then stacked one over the other, and carefully placed in the steamer. It is then covered with another blackened pot.
The steaming process

Steaming of idlis is done on a cloth covered mud pot. The use of firewood provides a special taste to the preparation. The steam ensures that these idlis end up with a texture that’s softer and much thinner than the conventional idli. A steaming pot of water is first covered with a jute mesh and later with a plain cotton cloth. Battered flour is poured over the cloth and then again covered with jute mesh. Once the batter is filled in three layers, the pot is fully covered with a large vessel. Idli is cooked in under three minutes. The earthy aroma enhances the taste of these idlis.

Once it is cooked, the idlis are served hot with coconut chutney, sambar and chammanthi podi, the spicy powder, made out of roasted rice, pepper, broken black gram, red chilli and coconut oil is the ideal combo for this delicacy.

seo.meta-title: Food writing: How cooking with local Australian produce helped cope with grief

story.headline: Recipes for resilience: How Cooking with local ingredients Down Under helped assuage a personal loss

2092048e-2a0e-4b7d-a3db-00c0e775fce3.headline: Mangaluru food safety officials seize halwa, other products prepared under unhygienic conditions

story.subheadline: When local produce meets nostalgic family recipes, food becomes more than sustenance: it becomes a lesson in openness and emotional recovery.
story.custom-slug: recipes-for-resilience

story-elements.text: For a long time, I’ve measured my travel plans in the form of a food checklist. A visit to the local market, a popular dish or cafe to try, pictures to share on social media, interesting market or supermarket finds to bring back and experiment with at home, a visit to the local library or independent bookstore for a unique food book find.

But at the crack of dawn, as I walked along the stretch between Altona beach Down Under and a coffee shop with my niece, with the sun painting the cloudy skies a faint peach, I realised that food and travel are intertwined beyond my own experience and understanding of culture and sentiment.

We ordered non-dairy coffees, mine a filter coffee and hers a turmeric latte shot through with freshly brewed San Pedro, and a delicious coconut pistachio crumb cake. It’s not something I set out to find through a list, but something I was leaning on based on lived experience with my niece — dipping bakery rusks into piping hot filter coffees at my parents’ home in Bengaluru, when she was small enough for me to pamper and big enough to share a conversation with.

I came here in the aftermath of losing my dad, and didn’t anticipate that any experience here, let alone food, would be where the grief would find its form of expression. But it has been a way of letting it flow and assuage me, one coffee, one meal at a time.
Focus on indigenous produce

There’s a growing body of research that food writers like me routinely dig into, especially centered around agrobiodiversity. Information on indigenous crops and ingredients and preparations that communities use in their everyday cooking — good buffers we have against an increasingly less predictable climate pattern. One of my favourite writers, Dan Saladino, wrote about how just three crops supply half the world’s calories, arguing that reclaiming a diverse food culture is vital for our future.

linked-story.headline: Mangaluru food safety officials seize halwa, other products prepared under unhygienic conditions

story-elements.text: Mangaluru food safety officials seize halwa, other products prepared under unhygienic conditions

For me, that diversity is clear when I’m standing in a distant produce aisle, thousands of kilometres from home, trying to recreate the taste of home from what’s actually growing there. Here, in Melbourne, that has translated into picking a fresh bunch of silver beet, more popularly known as chard in the West, in place of dantina soppu, and finding that the end product, majjige huli, doesn’t lose anything for the substitution. In fact, it possibly gains something — proof that a food tradition can be kept alive by staying flexible enough to meet a new one in a new land, half-way.

If you’ve read Braiding Sweetgrass, which, in my opinion, is a book that keeps on teaching — you’re no stranger to Robin Wall Kimmerer’s idea that the land’s gifts are given freely, but only really received when we respond with gratitude and give something back in turn. Visiting and staying with family in Australia and New Zealand over the years has taught me that lesson in small ways: to cook with sincerity using what grows here, what the soil and season are willing to offer, rather than importing every ingredient from home.
Free from tyranny of checklists

Being with family through this loss has mattered more than any one recipe I can single out. I’ve allowed myself to be comforted by cooking something simple and familiar instead of chasing the authentic version of the place. I’ve warmed up to the belief by now that this too is its own kind of resilience — comfort food rebuilding me enough to keep going. Do I rough it out sometimes and grit my teeth through unfamiliarity with the unnecessary desire to prove something?

Yes, but overall, my takeaway is that this experience is shaping how I want to write about and teach food going forward — less about ticking off a checklist focused on a land or cuisine’s top hits, and more about what it means to feed myself with a sense of honesty and openness about what it means for me in the moment, wherever I’ve landed. If that isn’t resilience, I don’t know what is. If that isn’t a way to heal, I don’t know a better one.
Recipe

Silver beet majjige huli
(Serves 4)

• One large bunch silver beet (chard) or any other greens like dantina soppu or chakota soppu, washed and chopped finely (stems and leaves)
• One cup thick curd, whisked smooth
• Two tbsp chana dal, soaked for 30 minutes
• A quarter cup of fresh grated coconut
• One tsp cumin seeds
• Two green chillies
• Half inch ginger
• A quarter tsp turmeric
• Salt to taste
For tempering: 1 tbsp coconut oil, ½ tsp mustard seeds, ⅛ tsp fenugreek seeds, a pinch of hing, a sprig of curry leaves, 1–2 dried red chillies

• Boil the silver beet in a large pot with very little water, until just tender.
• Grind the soaked chana dal, coconut, cumin, chillies, and ginger with a  little water into a smooth, thick paste.
• Stir the paste into the cooked greens, add salt and simmer for about 5 minutes until the raw dal smell is gone.
• Turn heat to low, pour in the whisked curd slowly, stirring constantly. Do not let it boil too much or for too long — just for a minute or two.
• Temper the mustard seeds, fenugreek, hing, curry leaves, and red chillies in hot oil; pour over the curry.
• Serve with hot rice and ideally, with a papad or two.
Ranjini is a communications professor, author, and podcaster, straddling many other worlds, in Bengaluru. She’s passionate about urban farming and sustainable living.

headline: What actually makes ultraprocessed foods unhealthy?

story.headline: What actually makes ultraprocessed foods unhealthy?
story.subheadline: The experts don't think it's realistic for most people to stop consuming ultraprocessed foods altogether.
story.summary: What actually makes ultraprocessed foods unhealthy?

story-elements.text: Scientists can't figure out why ultraprocessed foods are unhealthy for us--and new studies suggest that the "processing" isn't the problem

For breakfast, instant oatmeal. For lunch, a turkey sandwich on whole wheat bread. For dinner, a pasta bake with mozzarella cheese, and for dessert, low-fat yogurt and dried fruits. This diet is quite healthy and meets federal dietary guidelines--yet almost all of the calories come from ultraprocessed foods.

In countries such as the U.S. and the U.K., ultraprocessed foods make up at least half of the average diet. Research from the past few years has linked eating a lot of them to heart disease, diabetes and early death. Those findings have put the foods on everyone's radar--including federal policymakers in the U.S., who put out new dietary guidelines this year telling the public to avoid highly processed foods. The idea is that the processing itself might have effects on the food that make it easier for us to eat much more of it without noticing and for our body to digest it quickly or even that certain added ingredients such as preservatives and emulsifiers might be affecting our gut and how we handle blood glucose levels.

But is the problem really the processing, or could it be the kinds of nutrients these highly processed foods tend to contain? Ultraprocessed foods are often laden with ingredients we're told to avoid, and new findings are adding to the evidence that it's the nutrient profile--such as low fiber content and high amounts of sugar and saturated fat--more than the processing that affects our health in the long run. This could explain the existence of "healthy" ultraprocessed foods, such as yogurt and whole-grain breads, and suggests that classifying foods based on processing is trickier than it seems because it could steer people away from foods that are possibly doing them no harm.

To find out whether all ultraprocessed foods are equally bad for us, a team at the National Institutes of Health looked at national dietary survey data from more than 5,000 people. The researchers identified foods already labeled as "ultraprocessed," according to a common food-classification system called Nova, and they checked whether they were also high in the things dietary guidelines tell us to cut back on: added sugar, salt, saturated fat, refined grains and alcohol.

Unsurprisingly, about 90 percent of the calories that people consumed from ultraprocessed foods came from items that were high in nutrients to avoid. The researchers linked these same foods to higher body mass index and body fat, elevated insulin levels and increased inflammation.

But notably, the ultraprocessed foods that contained fewer nutrients to avoid, such as canned beans and vegetables, low-sugar yogurt, diet sodas and low-fat products, weren't correlated with the same adverse health indicators. This result suggests that the health effects linked to ultraprocessed foods might derive from their nutrition profile--although the observational nature of the data makes it difficult to identify what's really behind the effects. The preliminary findings were presented at the American Society for Nutrition's July meeting.

Leah Lipsky, the study's lead author and a nutrition epidemiologist at the NIH, says the research doesn't mean people should eat a diet composed of only ultraprocessed foods with a better nutritional profile. "That's not quite what we're trying to get at," she says. Instead it suggests that the "ultraprocessed" framing isn't the best place to begin to understand a food's health effects. Lipsky also notes that some food manufacturers are reformulating ultraprocessed foods to market them as more healthful choices. But this approach misses the point, she says. "We really want to try to encourage people to eat more foods straight from the produce section" rather than relying on the "ultraprocessed versus nonultraprocessed" distinction.

Other large studies have also found that the link between ultraprocessed foods and disease risk is being driven by specific types of foods within the category. In particular, processed meats and cheese, as well as sweetened drinks, pose more of a risk, whereas foods such as breads, cereals and plant-based alternatives don't have the same associations with poor health. In 2023 a team at the U.S. Department of Agriculture built a menu that met federal dietary guidelines even though almost all of the calories came from ultraprocessed foods, adding weight to the idea that not all these foods are necessarily "bad."

Yet some evidence suggests the processing still matters. In 2019 another team at the NIH reported on 20 adults who ate ultraprocessed and unprocessed diets with food options carefully matched for calories, sugar, fat, salt and fiber. On the ultraprocessed diet, people ate roughly 500 extra calories a day and gained weight. In a similar study reported last year, researchers in England gave 50 people two different diets, both designed to meet the U.K. healthy-eating guidance but with one consisting of ultraprocessed foods and the other of minimally processed ones. Both caused weight loss, but people lost twice as many pounds on average on the minimally processed diet.

These studies, though short in duration, all point in the same direction, says Marion Nestle, professor emerita of nutrition at New York University: people have better health outcomes when they eat less ultraprocessed diets. Ultraprocessing physically alters the structure of some food molecules, she explains. Corn chips, for example, start as whole corn kernels, which get cooked in an alkaline solution to loosen the hull and ground into wet dough that is then formed into shapes and fried. This process eliminates the physical structure of the corn and creates something resembling a predigested food--which the gut digests faster than it would a whole food, Nestle says.

Whether it is how soft and easy to chew these foods are or their tasty combinations of fat, salt and sugar, "something about [ultraprocessed foods] encourages people to eat more without realizing it," Nestle says.

The processing and the nutrient makeup may both matter. David Julian McClements, a food scientist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, says the foods that end up in the ultraprocessed group tend to be the ones nutritionists have been warning about for decades anyway--those that have been broadly but imprecisely referred to as "junk food." He thinks the processing does have real effects, but they're "much smaller than the [nutritional]-composition effects."

The experts don't think it's realistic for most people to stop consuming ultraprocessed foods altogether. "Most people haven't got the time, the energy, the money or the inclination" to cook from scratch, McClements says. His suggestion is for scientists to work out which processed foods cause harm and why, redesign those specifically and then test whether the redesign actually helps--although such trials are slow and expensive.
Nestle's advice to us is simpler. "Eating less junk food is good health advice," she says.

story.headline: The obbattu: Tracing the layered history of Karnataka’s festive sweet
story.subheadline: From medieval culinary texts to regional variations made with lentils, coconut, peanuts and sweet potato, obbattu has evolved over centuries, reflecting Karnataka’s diverse food traditions.

story-elements.text: The festive season is here, and with that comes the prospect of habbada oota — an elaborate spread for the occasion. The obbattu or holige, the Karnataka version of Maharashtra’s púran poli , Tamil Nadu’s poli, and Andhra and Telangana’s bobbatlu/oliga/bhakshyam is an invariable presence.

What then is the origin story of the obbattu? K T Achaya’s Indian Food: A Historical Companion points to 12th-century King Someshwara’s Manasollasa, where he mentions “mandakas”, made of wheat flour, and stuffed with “various fillings”. Achaya goes on to write that honey would yield “madhumestaka” or “madhushirshaka” while “jaggery and mashed dhals would give pahalikas or põlikas”. He also points out that the word, poorana (stuffing) could be the precusor to puran poli. Achaya references works like Lokopakara of 11th-century poet and minister Chavundaraya and Soopa Shastra of 16th-century King Mangarasa III of the Chengalva dynasty while tracing the evolution of the sweet and its variations such as mandige and húrige. The word holige found mention only after the 16th-century, according to Achaya’s book. His work also mentions the suruli holige made in parts of North Karnataka.

The word obbattu comes comes from ubbu (puff up) and attu (crepe/rolled out dough with the stuffing), according to Anusha Venkatesh, founder of The Õle Project, which documents Karnataka’s cuisine and hosts supper clubs. The permutations and combinations of hoorana (stuffing) and kanaka (the wrap) make for different kinds of obbattu. The stuffing could be made from coconut (kayi) and jaggery, dals (kadale and togari bele), and sesame (yellu/til). There is North Karnataka’s shenga holige, with a stuffing of crushed peanuts and sesame, made for occasions like Yellu Amavasye, an agrarian celebration. Khova, made by reducing milk, and stuffed to make holige, is also popular in North Karnataka, she observes.
Regional variations

Anusha explains that the sweet potato (genasu) holige is popular in parts of the state, including the Malnad region. Post-monsoon, a purple tinged variety of sweet potato is harvested and used to make holige, she adds. Native varieties of pumpkin are also used to make stuffings for holige. Geography, climatic conditions and agricultural practices play a key role in these variations. For Smruthi, a food content creator based out of Mangaluru, a cherished dish that her mother made was the jackfruit seed holige. “Instead of letting the seeds go to waste, my mother would turn them into a rich, comforting sweet holige,” she recalls. The sweet has been constantly reimagined over the centuries. A popular Kannada saying likens daydreaming to the imaginary relishing of the mandige but this festive season, relish a fresh mandige or obbattu, hot off the griddle.
