headline: Odisha on a platter: Exploring the traditions, flavours and culinary heritage of Odia cuisine

seo.meta-description: Odia cuisine: Discover the rich culinary heritage of Odisha, featuring sacred temple food from Puri, coastal seafood, simple dalma and tribal forest flavours.
seo.meta-title: Odisha on a platter: Exploring the traditions, flavours and culinary heritage of Odia cuisine

story.headline: Odisha on a platter: Exploring the traditions, flavours and culinary heritage of Odia cuisine
story.subheadline: Odia cuisine is not shaped by a single tradition — its many flavours have been defined from the region's forests, sea and rivers, apart from temples and royal kitchens.

story-elements.text: To understand Odia cuisine is to discover a cuisine shaped not by a single tradition, but by an entire civilisation. Its flavours have emerged from temples and royal kitchens, fishing communities and village homes, fertile plains and ancient forests, rivers and the sea. Faith, geography, seasons, and memory have all found their way into the Odia kitchen. This is perhaps why Odisha’s food is so rich and diverse: its cuisine is not one story, but many stories woven together over generations.

At the heart of this culinary inheritance is the living temple-food tradition of Odisha, above all the sacred kitchen of the Jagannath Temple in Puri. Here, food transcends nourishment. It becomes an offering, an act of devotion and a manifestation of the divine. The ancient idea of Anna Brahma, food as sacred, and as Brahman, runs deep in Odia culture. The preparation, offering and sharing of mahaprasad, embody a tradition that has survived through centuries, preserving not merely recipes but a profound philosophy of food.
Beyond the temple tradition

Yet the extraordinary feature of this temple tradition is that it has never remained confined to the temple. Its influence flows naturally into Odia homes. Khechudi, dalma, kanika, khata and pitha belong to a culinary world where the distinction between ritual food and everyday food can be remarkably fluid. The sacred and the domestic meet at the dining table, allowing culinary traditions to travel from temple to home and from one generation to the next.

story-elements.title: Manda pitha, steamed dumpling made for festive occasions.

story-elements.text: When simplicity is depth

Odia cooking also reveals the remarkable depth that can emerge from simplicity. It rarely seeks to overwhelm the palate with an abundance of spices. Instead, mustard, cumin, ginger, garlic, turmeric, green chilli, panch phutana, mustard oil, coconut, curd, and souring agents such as ambula are used with a measured hand. The intention is often to enhance rather than conceal the principal ingredient. A simple preparation of fish, lentils or vegetables can therefore possess extraordinary layers of flavour. Machha haldi pani, dalma, santula, dahi baigana, besara and ambula rai demonstrate how restraint can itself become a culinary art.

story-elements.title: Chakuli pitha, a fermented rice crepe.

story-elements.text: Rice, naturally, lies at the heart of this food culture. But rice in Odisha is never merely rice.
It is transformed into pakhala, kanika, khechudi, chakuli, chuda, khai and an extraordinary range of pithas. Each form carries its own texture, flavour and cultural association.
Pitha, especially, belongs to the rhythm of Odia life appearing with particular seasons, festivals, rituals and family occasions.
To eat a pitha can therefore be to taste not merely an ingredient, but a season, a memory and a tradition.
Culinary wisdom

Ancient techniques of fermentation, drying and preservation further enrich this culinary vocabulary. Pakhala is perhaps the best-known expression of fermentation, but the tradition extends to fermented batters, dried fish and vegetables, ambula and many other preserved ingredients. These were practical techniques born from intimate knowledge of the land and its seasons. They allowed communities to preserve the abundance of one season for another, while simultaneously creating distinctive flavours. What began as necessity became culinary wisdom.

Odisha’s geography adds yet another layer. The Chilika Lake, network of rivers, and the state’s coastline have given rise to a food culture deeply connected with prawns, crab and fish (both fresh and dried). Coastal cooking often brings together these ingredients with mustard, turmeric, souring agents and local vegetables, creating preparations that are delicate, earthy and distinctly different from the richer, heavier gravies found elsewhere in India.

Move inland, and another Odisha emerges. In the hills and forests of Koraput, Malkangiri, Rayagada, Kandhamal, Kalahandi, Keonjhar and Sundargarh, indigenous food traditions reflect the extraordinary biodiversity of the region. Millets, tubers, forest greens, bamboo, mushrooms, indigenous rice, leafy vegetables, pulses and forest produce become important elements of the diet. Smoking, roasting, fermenting, and other traditional techniques reveal generations of knowledge about the land and its bounty.
A coming together
Perhaps this multiplicity is Odisha’s greatest culinary strength. There is no single dish that can define Odia cuisine. Its identity lies precisely in the coexistence of many traditions.

A culinary journey through Odisha can take us from mahaprasad in Puri to seafood beside Chilika; from pakhala served in a village home to a royal Mayurbhanj mutton preparation; from delicate pithas made in a coastal kitchen to millet and forest foods of Koraput or Malkangiri.

headline: Breaking bread: A taste of tradition in Georgia

seo.meta-description: Georgian bread: Discover the rich culinary history behind traditional clay oven baking, regional varieties like Imeruli khachapuri, and ancient wheat roots tracing back eight thousand years across local regions.
seo.meta-title: Breaking bread: A taste of tradition in Georgia

story.headline: Breaking bread: A taste of tradition in Georgia

59144fad-0237-4a10-ad02-4e8ff212b4ec.headline: A snack worth a little spanking

story.subheadline: The classic Imeruli khachapuri, originating in Imereti, is round and filled with cheese. Megruli khachapuri from Samegrelo has cheese stuffed inside as well as melted over the top.

story-elements.text:
The dough felt surprisingly soft in my hands as I tried to stretch it into the elongated shape I had seen Georgian bakers make effortlessly. Under the watchful eye of Ms Eto Iobashvili at Giuaani, a family-run winery in Kakheti, I shaped my first Georgian bread before attempting the trickier part — placing it inside the tone, the traditional clay oven.

With a few pointers from Eto, the dough was slapped against the scorching inner wall, where it clung precariously before slowly puffing and browning. Minutes later, I was tearing into warm, freshly baked bread, crisp at the edges and soft and chewy within.

“For Georgian bread, you need high-quality bread flour, fresh yeast, warm milk and a pinch of salt. The quality of these ingredients is crucial, as they directly impact the flavour and texture of the final product,” says Eto. What seemed like a fun bread-making masterclass, however, was an introduction to a culinary tradition with remarkably ancient roots.

linked-story.headline: A snack worth a little spanking

story-elements.text: A snack worth a little spanking

According to Georgia’s Ministry of Culture, a new international study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences identifies Georgia as one of the world’s oldest independent centres of origin for bread wheat (Triticum aestivum L). The research draws on archaeological evidence from the Neolithic sites of Gadachrili Gora and Shulaveris Gora, dating back nearly 8,000 years.
As I travelled across the country, I began to realise that bread here comes in many shapes, textures and character.

In Tbilisi, I encountered shotis puri again at Republic 24, an upscale café, where the traditional bread sits comfortably alongside a contemporary dining experience. “Foreign travellers love shoti because they find the whole experience authentic, especially seeing bread being baked in a traditional clay oven even at an upscale café,” says Sava Kamarauli, a server at the cafe.

Fresh from the oven, the bread needs little embellishment. Its crust gives way to a chewy centre, making it tempting enough to tear and eat on its own. Yet, another Georgian bread on the same table intrigued mw. It arrived golden, warm and generously filled with cheese: khachapuri.
When cheese meets bread

Calling khachapuri “cheese bread” hardly does justice to it. Almost every region seems to have its own interpretation of the bread, shaped by local ingredients and culinary traditions. The classic Imeruli khachapuri, originating in Imereti, is round and filled with cheese. Megruli khachapuri from Samegrelo has cheese stuffed inside as well as melted over the top.

Perhaps the most recognisable is Adjaruli khachapuri from the Black Sea region of Adjara. Shaped like a boat, it comes filled with molten cheese and topped with an egg yolk and a generous knob of butter. Eating it involves a small ritual: the egg and butter are stirred into the hot cheese before pieces of the crust are torn off by hand and dipped into the creamy centre.

Even the cheeses, grains, and methods used to prepare the bread are not the same across the nation. At Café Salve, I came across lobiani, a bread stuffed with seasoned red beans, and mchadi, the rustic cornbread popular in western Georgia. Then there is nazuki, a subtly sweet, aromatic bread associated particularly with Surami, where roadside stalls tempt passing travellers with freshly baked loaves. A

t Vardzia Restaurant, I try meskhetian bread, from southern Georgia, which reflects the region’s old baking traditions, and chvishtari, a hearty cornbread enriched with cheese, giving it a crisp exterior and a warm, gooey centre.
A supra gathering

But perhaps the best place to understand the importance of bread is not a bakery at all. It is at a supra. “A Georgian supra has the warmth of gathering around a table at home,” says local guide Ia Gebrandze. “There is homemade bread, wine and an abundance of dishes to share, but what really matters is being together. Food is our way of welcoming people and making them feel part of the family.”

headline: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

seo.meta-description: Botanical cocktails: Top Indian mixologists are reviving traditional flowers like mahua and rose to craft lighter, sustainable and story-driven drinks in contemporary bars.
seo.meta-title: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

story.headline: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

7fa7539d-4d77-43fb-a985-14e2ca035769.headline: The world is drinking less, but India is bucking the trend

story.subheadline: Beyond the decorative rim, flowers have become the new flavour baseline in contemporary mixology.
story.custom-slug: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

story-elements.text: “It started not as a floral exploration, but as a love letter to Delhi — its culture, history, and distinct flavours,” recalls co-founder and alcobev pioneer Minakshi Singh on the genesis of Sidecar’s signature Dear Delhi menu.

Among the menu’s defining creations was Mehrauli, a drink inspired by the historic Phool Walon Ki Sair festival and built around an old-school, floral-infused gin. The team also created Batik, pairing Tanqueray London Dry Gin with a striking top float of blue pea-infused wine.

Incidentally, Sidecar, among Asia’s top 50 bars, wasn’t the first to revive the floral cocktail culture; the now-closed Armenian cuisine-themed restaurant Lavaash By Saby did so back in 2015 when founder Chef Sabyasachi Gorai recreated the tribal mahua drink for the modern palate.

The drink, called Mahua Mehul, used mahua steeped in gin or vodka to craft a delicious, fragrant nectar. The drink was crafted, “not just for the cultural history but for the mahua’s versatility as a traditional food, a flower with medicinal properties and its flavours,” he recalls.

linked-story.headline: The world is drinking less, but India is bucking the trend

story-elements.text: The world is drinking less, but India is bucking the trend

Manan Sen, Bar Manager, Sienna Calcutta, crafted mahua into a drink that “honoured the legacy while blending it with contemporary bar techniques.” While Chef Saby’s creation was served in a copper bucket with house-made gummy bear candies, Manan’s iteration incorporated mahua as a syrup and an infusion to craft a light-on-the-palate, boozy tippler.

story-elements.title: Agua de Jamaica (a hibiscus-based drink) at the Sanchez Restaurante & Agave Room.

story-elements.text: For Sanchez Restaurante & Agave Room, Agua De Jamaica, a refreshing hibiscus cooler, is also seeing a beverage-to-cocktail revolution. The idea, says culinary director Chef Vikas Seth, “isn’t to take away anything from the popular hibiscus drink paired with most Mexican food, but to give it that little tipsiness that makes it a perfect daytime indulgence.”

For Plus Nine One, it was Call for Rose. The drink, featuring a damask rose-infused vodka and clarified rose cordial blend, favours botanical complexity over cloying sweetness. Created as an ode to the Mughal and Persian obsession with rose-based beverages, the drink, says bar manager Naveen Nautiyal, “is made with house-made rose cordial with citrus peels, and is paired with rose wine, lime zest-infused vodka and ginger ale.”
Not a trend but a return

What has sparked the renewed interest in flower-based cocktails? Globally, the catalyst was the launch of St-Germain elderflower liqueur in 2007 that earned it the nickname ‘bartender’s ketchup’ for its versatility. In India, however, the revival had more to do with the evolution of bartending itself, observes Stormy founder Yangdup Lama. “Floral cocktails are subtler and lighter on flavours. When played right, they can transform into delicious and delicate long drinks like Hi-balls, Collins and well-balanced Martinis.”

According to Mayur Marne of Cobbler & Crew, “the change is more aptitudinal — flowers are now viewed as a core structural ingredient to build the drink around, rather than just a visual afterthought. Add to that is the guest demand for lighter, fresher, and more elegant drinks that evoke memories while being easy on the palate.”
Manan concurs. “More than its visual representation or flavour profile, a floral cocktail can become a deeply personal experience, connecting people to places, traditions, and moments they cherish.”

Adds Varun Sudhakar of Moss Xperia, “Floral cocktails are a delightful way not just to tell great stories but, when thoughtfully crafted, can achieve that perfect balance between traditional healing properties and pleasure.”

Most good tasting floral cocktails, says Yangdup, “are not only minimally designed but also incorporate ingredients like syrups, shrubs, cold infusions, teas and tinctures, making them one of the most elegant yet sustainable forms of crafting drinks.”
New iterations vis-à-vis the old

The canvas has remained the same — rose, elderflower, mogra, jasmine and marigold with a few exceptions, observes Varun, explaining, “what has changed is the construction. If I am using dried rose petals, I will choose to base it as a gin cocktail, while for jasmine, it may be a good rum or whisky.”

For Yangdup, “it depends first on the spirit, which is then matched not only with the floral flavour but also the variety — fresh or dried — followed by the garnish that can add not just the visual narrative but upgrade the drinking pleasure.”

story-elements.title: Persian Bling at The Grammar Room.

story-elements.text: Regional mixologist Ram Kumar of The Grammar Room begins with the flower flavour profile. “I then build the drink around a complementary spirit and flavour memory. The aim is to capture the essence without overpowering the drink, so it uses gentle infusions, light syrups, and teas, making use of floral ingredients with restraint for balance and freshness.”

Mayur explains that he begins with flavour first, followed by the spirit that complements the notes, and then the technique. “For me, the ratio of a good floral cocktail is 70 per cent aroma and taste, and 30 per cent visual appeal,” he adds.

headline: Vegetarian, but make it fancy: Bengaluru's new-age dining scene

seo.meta-description: Vegetarian Restaurants: Discover how upscale eateries across South Bengaluru are changing the culinary scene by serving experimental global fusion food, moving far beyond traditional menus to attract crowds.

story.headline: Vegetarian, but make it fancy: Bengaluru's new-age dining scene

d1aec702-9485-4dc0-8a5e-d2879e431f6c.headline: Traditional Kashmiri Pandit cuisine finds a place on Delhi's food map

story.subheadline: More spaces in South Bengaluru now serve experimental food beyond paneer and mushroom.

story-elements.text: It’s the middle of a busy weekday, and Eatinn Love Trattoria in Jayanagar is almost completely full. The 56-seater focuses on a vegetarian-only menu of pizza and pasta. Though it has been around for eight years, it was reopened in its new upscale avatar only four months ago.
It is one among a number of vegetarian experimental and upscale restaurants that have been opened in the city over the last year or two.

In South Bengaluru alone, names like Kalpaney, Cable Car, Ale, Moai and Continuum draw a large crowd, especially over the weekends. Raghotham V, a 40-year-old film enthusiast and coffee connoisseur, visited Kalpaney, J P Nagar, last weekend with 15 of his cousins.

linked-story.headline: Traditional Kashmiri Pandit cuisine finds a place on Delhi's food map

story-elements.text: Traditional Kashmiri Pandit cuisine finds a place on Delhi's food map

“We wanted to try a pure-vegetarian fine-dining restaurant and chose Kalpaney for its Indian fusion menu,” he shares. Guava chilli pani-puri, Thai yellow curry dim sum, avocado cheesy nigiri, and curd rice were some of the dishes he sampled. Priced between Rs 350 and Rs 500, he found it to be equal to the prices at any non-vegetarian restaurant.

“All drinks are non-alcoholic, and the signature drinks were around Rs 525, which puts them on par with the price of cocktails,” he notes.

Chef Sombir, co-founder, shares that he wanted to explore Indian vegetarian food “in a way that felt exciting and relevant for today”. “India has such a rich vegetarian food culture. Every region has its own ingredients, techniques and flavours. Kalpaney came from the idea of celebrating that diversity while presenting it in a contemporary and playful way,” he explains.

On the menu, one will spot jhol momos, and dahi bhalla with feta, alongside Mysore chilli broccoli, chilli cheese dim sum, and California blue pea roll. These are their most frequently ordered dishes, too. “The common thread is that they have strong Indian and regional flavours, but are presented in a slightly unexpected way,” he notes.

After working at multiple upscale restaurant chains in Bengaluru, Alister Braganza and chef Saurabh Arora, teamed up to open Continuum, also located in J P Nagar. It is described as a restaurant that “reimagines vegetarian cuisine through a global perspective”. The space reflects the name, with continuity and wave-like patterns recurring through its design.
Unexplored cuisine

When Alister and his partner were mulling over opening their own restaurant, it struck them that vegetarian cuisine was largely unexplored. “Most places have extensive non-vegetarian options. Vegetarian food probably comprises 20-30% of most menus,” he says, adding that they were looking to create something that would be popular and would not fail.

The menu here changes every three months, and some favourites include thecha paneer, gol gappa with jalapeno water, and charcoal noodles. Their ‘community menu’ also allows customers to share their family recipes. “We give them a form to fill out and give us their recipes. We have had people share their grandmother’s or mother’s recipes. And whatever we find interesting, we try to replicate it with our own tweaks,” he shares.

At the Trattoria, founder Niharika imported an oven from Italy to make pala romana pizzas, which are characterised by their rectangular base. “It’s a sourdough base, but it is crisp, which is what sets them apart,” says Niharika, who also imports the flour from Italy. The vespa and verdure pesto pizzas and the cacio e pepe are some of the favourites.
Pricing on par

Most of these places will set one back by about Rs 2,000. They draw families, young couples, and working professionals alike. The restaurateurs all agree that the location plays an important role in their success, too. “South Bengaluru is known for its large traditional, pure vegetarian population, and we are fully booked on weekends,” says Niharika.

“Pure vegetarian has traditionally meant darshini-style eateries with limited menus. A fine-dining restaurant with an exclusive vegetarian menu allows vegetarian diners to explore global cuisines like Asian, Italian or Mediterranean more freely,” Raghotham concludes.

story.subheadline: Food has been at the centre of debate in political and diplomatic circles in recent times. Purabi Shridhar and Sanghita Singh talk to the families, personal cooks, and chefs of India's prime ministers and unravel recipes and anecdotes. Here are some excerpts.

On the menu:
The PMs’ choice

story-elements.text: Purabi Shridhar and Sanghita Singh

On Rajiv Gandhi who served as PM between October 31, 1984 and December 2, 1989, Mohsina Kidwai, whose family were friends with the Nehru-Gandhis says, “Rajiv Gandhi loved kebabs, especially shaami and galauti; and loved kheer.”
Mutton kebab

Ingredients: Mutton, 1 kg, minced; chana dal, 250 gm, washed and soaked; ginger, 1 and a 1/2 inches long; garlic, 6–7 pods; green chilli, 1–2; onions, 2; garam masala (black pepper, cardamom, clove, cinnamon finely ground), one tablespoon; salt, to taste; coriander (fresh), 2 tbsps, finely minced; oil, to shallow fry.

Put mutton, chana dal, ginger, garlic, green chilli and onions in a pressure cooker. Add a little water and cook for 2–3 whistles. Let it cool down and ensure that the water dries up. Or put the whole thing in a thick-bottomed saucepan, put water to cover, and when it comes to a boil, let it simmer until the water dries up. Grind the whole mixture on a grinding stone until it becomes a fine paste. Put in the garam masala, salt to taste, and fresh coriander before mixing thoroughly.
Make small balls of the mixture and flatten each into a kebab. Shallow fry on a tawa on low flame on both sides till they are done. Serve hot with coriander/mint chutney.
(Recipe courtesy: Mohsina Kidwai’s family cook, Ismail)

On V P Singh, who served as the PM between December 2, 1989 and November 10, 1990, Sita Kumari, his wife, says: "One distinct trait he had was that he disliked hot meals. If the meals were very hot, he would put the bowl in some water to cool it down."

Safed maas

Ingredients: Mutton, 1/2 kg; salt, to taste; ghee, 120 gm; curd, 120 gm; seeds of dried red chilli, ground with water, 12 gm; ginger, 12 gm, peeled and shredded; almonds, blanched and ground with water, 12 gm; khoya, 30 gm; poppy seeds (khuskhus) ground with a little water, 12 gm; coconut, ground with water, 12 gm; milk, 120 ml; rose water, 15 ml; lime juice, 7 ml; cardamom seeds, powdered, 11 gm; deseeded red chillies and slightly boiled green chilli for garnish.

Put meat in a heavy-bottomed saucepan (dekchi) with a little salt. Submerge in water and boil for about 5 minutes. Remove from heat, drain the water, and wash the meat twice in fresh water. In the same saucepan, heat ghee, add the meat along with curd, add salt to taste, ground red chilli seeds, and shredded ginger. Cover with water and let it cook till the meat is tender. Ensure that the water should be just enough so that when the meat becomes tender, all of it has evaporated.

Next add the almond paste, khoya, poppy seeds paste, ground coconut and milk. Stir it all thoroughly. Cover and cook on low heat in dum style (after putting the lid, seal its edges with wheat dough to stop steam from escaping). Cook till the gravy becomes thick and the ghee floats on top. Then, add rose water, lime juice and powdered cardamom. Garnish with deseeded red chillies and slightly boiled green chilli.
(Recipe courtesy: VP Singh's family)
On P V Narasimha Rao, who served as the PM between June 21, 1991 and May 16, 1996, his daughter Vani says, "He always ended his meal with curd rice and chintakaya pachhadi!"
Chintakaya thokku pachhadi (tamarind pickle)
Ingredients: Tamarind (tender green with hard seeds), 500 gm; salt, 100 gm; turmeric powder, one teaspoon

Ingredients for tempering: oil, 2 tablespoons; mustard seeds, 2 teaspoons; cumin, 1 teaspoon; fenugreek seeds, 1/2 teaspoon; chana dal (Bengal gram), 1 tablespoon; urad dal (husked black lentil), 1 teaspoon; green chillies 4, slit; red chilli (dried), three; sugar or jaggery, 1/2 teaspoon; curry leaves, a handful; asafoetida, a pinch

Wash raw tamarind thoroughly with water and dry them on a kitchen towel for 4–5 hours until completely dry. Deseed and cut the dried tamarind into small pieces and grind coarsely on a traditional stone-grinder for an authentic taste. While grinding, gradually add salt and turmeric powder.
Store the chintakaya thokku in an airtight jar. After three days, it becomes a little soft.

Grind it once again into a fine paste. For tempering, heat one tablespoon oil in a pan. Add cumin, one teaspoon mustard seeds and fenugreek seeds, and when they start spluttering, add chana and urad dals.

Fry until they turn golden brown. Add green and two red chillies. Switch off the flame and allow the ingredients to cool. Grind them all in a blender. Then add chintakaya thokku to it and grind to a smooth consistency, adding sugar/jaggery while grinding. In another pan, heat the remaining oil.
Add remaining mustard seeds, curry leaves and the red chilli. When the mustard seeds start to crackle, add asafoetida and switch off the flame. Add the tempering to the chutney and mix well.
(Recipe courtesy: Vani Dayakar Rao)

On H D Deve Gowda, who served as PM between June 1, 1996 and April 21, 1997, the book says: "At 7 RCR, it was usually upma, idli, dosa, or rice roti with chutney for breakfast, raagi balls, curd and curry for lunch, and chapatis/rice rotis served with curry, followed by a platter of fruits for dinner."
Raagi ball
Ingredients: Raagi flour, 1 cup; water, 2 cups; ghee, 1 teaspoon

Add one teaspoon of raagi flour in a vessel of water and mix well. Put this on a gas stove on medium heat and bring to boil. Lower the flame and gradually add the remaining raagi flour and cook for two–three minutes, all the while mixing well with a wooden spatula. Turn off the heat and add ghee. Then make a ball with your hands. Serve hot with vegetable curry (one ball serves 1).
Vegetable curry

Ingredients: Arhar dal, 1 and a 1/2 cups; fenugreek (methi) leaves, 1 bunch; dhantu (amaranth leaves, if available), 1 bunch; spinach, 1 bunch; radish, 1/2, cut into long slender pieces; onion, 1, chopped finely; tomato, 1, chopped; water, 3 cups or enough to cover the dal and greens; salt to taste

Ingredients for tempering: refined oil, 2 tablespoons; Mustard seeds, 1/2 teaspoon; onion, 1, finely chopped; garlic, few cloves, chopped finely or crushed; red chillies, 2; curry leaves, 6–7; turmeric powder, 1/2 teaspoon; sambar powder, 2 teaspoons; coconut, fresh grated, 2 tablespoons (optional)

Soak dal for half an hour and boil it with the green leafy vegetables, radish and salt in an open vessel along with tomato and onion. Once the dal is cooked, keep it aside. In a separate wok, add oil and, when it becomes hot, add mustard seeds, finely chopped onion, garlic, red chillies, curry leaves, turmeric powder and sambar powder. Add grated coconut (optional). Finally, add the dal and the greens mix and cook for a minute till all the spices mix well. Serve hot with a raagi ball or rice.

On Atal Bihari Vajpayee, who served as PM thrice: 1996: 13 days; 1998 to 1999: 13 months; and October 13 to May 22, 2004, veteran chef M S Gupta says, "Sometimes, food used to go from Ashoka Hotel to his house and we always sent him fish."
Golden fried prawns

story-elements.title: Golden fried prawns with chilli dip.

story-elements.text: Ingredients: King prawns, 220 gm; oil, 1 litre; refined flour, 120 gm; corn flour, 80 gm; baking powder, 15 gm; salt, 5 gm; white pepper powder, 3 gm; sugar, 3 gm; ginger, 10 gm, chopped into small bits, preferably with a Chinese cleaver knife; garlic, 10 gm, chopped into small bits, preferably with a Chinese cleaver knife; chilli paste, 20 gm; vinegar, 2 ml; potato starch, 20 gm
Clean, deshell, and devein the king prawns. To make the marinade, mix corn flour, 30 ml of refined oil and salt. Marinate the prawns in the mixture and refrigerate for 6 hours.
For the batter: In a clean and dry bowl, take the refined flour, corn flour and baking powder and mix well. Add salt, white pepper powder, sugar and mix it with water to make a smooth batter.

Add 100 ml refined oil to the batter and let the batter rest for 30 minutes. Heat the rest of the 70 ml oil in a wok controlling the temperature at around 180 degrees. Dip the prawns in batter, drain thoroughly, and slowly lower them into the oil. Allow the prawns to attain a golden hue before draining them on kitchen paper.
(Recipe courtesy: The Taj Mahal Hotel, Delhi)

headline: Kitchen without a homeland: How Partition altered the flavours of Sindhi food

seo.meta-description: Sindhi Cuisine: How the Partition altered traditional flavours, lost hyper-local ingredients from the River Indus, and reshaped food habits of displaced refugees across India.
seo.meta-title: Sindhi Food: How the Partition Altered the Flavours of Traditional Cuisine

story.headline: Kitchen without a homeland: How Partition altered the flavours of Sindhi food

story.subheadline: In the second part of the series on the impact of the Partition on culinary practices in India, DH looks at how the Sindhi community not only became stateless and scattered but also saw a loss of cooking practices, lack of access to ingredients and a change in food habits.
story.custom-slug: Kitchen without a homeland: How Partition altered the flavours of Sindhi food

story-elements.text: In Sadhana’s first film, ‘Abana’ (1958), the song ‘Daal chola dabal’ became a map of a homeland left behind. To many, it was simply a catchy tune about street food. But to Sindhi refugees sitting in cinema halls, names like Radhe Mal and Moti Mal (food vendors) brought back flavours and memories of a place they were forced to leave just a decade earlier. While the song captured the joy of the streets, kitchen tables of their makeshift homes dependent on government ration told a different story. When a community is forced to leave its land, what happens to the food that cannot travel with it?
In a stateless India

For the Sindhi community, Partition meant losing not just homes but an entire province. Stateless and scattered, much was lost in the struggle to rebuild. “Sindhis didn’t have the best time settling, and the immediate need was to find a means of livelihood and get their children into good schools. Trying to retain their lifestyle and eating habits became secondary,” culinarian Sapna Ajwani notes.

The Indus region and Sindh’s arid climate shaped a cuisine dominated by meat and fish. But after settling in different parts of India, some Sindhis in vegetarian communities turned to the same practice to fit in — a loss compounded by discrimination and difficulties finding housing. “Back in Sindh, there was a lot of give-and-take with the Muslim community; our lifestyle was influenced by them,” says culinarian Alka Keswani.

story-elements.title: Palli macchi, fish cooked in a sauce of mashed palli, sorrel leaves, and green garlic shallots.

story-elements.text: The rise of spiritual movements also propelled vegetarianism — displaced Sindhis turned towards such communities for a sense of belonging. With the emphasis on a sattvic lifestyle, vegetarianism became a marker of moral resilience.
Lost ingredients

At the centre of the Sindhi way of living was River Indus; its seasonal floods, changing currents, and rich ecosystem defining ingredients and cooking philosophies. The migration deprived access to hyper-local ingredients tied to this ecosystem. One such was the Indus palla (a type of ilish), a migratory species.

In her book ‘Sindh: Sindhi Recipes and Stories from a Forgotten Land’, Sapna lists unique palla recipes like bhaapwari macchi (steamed fish), palli macchi (fish in green chickpea leaves), seyal macchi, (braised), wadi ji macchi (dough encased and cooked in sand pits) and kok pallo (twice cooked), among others. After Partition, the fish became difficult to incorporate into everyday cooking. Vegetarianism and rising costs were some reasons. Practicality also shaped what made it to the table. “The mother perhaps did not want to spend time helping the kids eat the palla. It was easier to give them pomfret or surmai, which was less bony,” Sapna says. The flooding of the Indus created vast marshlands where lotus grew wild. Its root / stem (bhee) and seeds became staples of Sindhi food. When Sapna visited Sindh for her book, she found lotus stems that were plump, juicy, and meaty. From everyday snacks and street food to wedding menus, the lotus stem was so ubiquitous that culinary historians describe it as the potato of Sindh. “Before potatoes took over the kitchen, the go-to starch was lotus stem,” Sapna says.

story-elements.image-attribution: Ming Tang Evans, food photographer for Sindh:Recipes and Stories from a Forgotten Land
story-elements.title: Phote mein gosht, meat cooked in a stew of cardamom and black pepper.

linked-story.headline: Memories that crossed the divide: The unspoken human cost and legacy of Partition

story-elements.text: Memories that crossed the divide: The unspoken human cost and legacy of Partition

Rice was shaped by Sindh’s waters. In the south-eastern part of the province, near the mouth of the Indus, pools of water supported rice cultivation. Red rice was among the varieties grown and consumed there but once they moved and settled in parts of Gujarat, Rajasthan and Mumbai, the practice of eating rice declined, according to Sapna.
Changing practices

While sai bhaji survived, it is now made using just spinach, observes Sapna. Sorrel, dill leaves, amaranth, and other foraged greens were also used traditionally, she adds. Foraging during the monsoon was also a big aspect of Sindhi life. The monsoon brought a variety of wild mushrooms, including huge edible ones (khumbi). Sapna’s aunt from Jodhpur reminisced about foraging for wild mushrooms during the first rain.

Foraging and drying vegetables were vital because nearly 60% of Sindh was arid. Turnips, apple gourds, mushrooms, and lotus stem were dried and stored, as were seasonal desert vegetables like kair (wild berry), sangri (desert bean) and kumat (seed pods), rehydrated for dishes like raabro tharparkar (in yoghurt sauce). Sapna also mentions palli (chickpea greens) and dadhri (snow peas), ingredients she rarely finds in India. Palli, with its sweet flavour, is cooked with fish or goat, while dadhri is boiled and eaten as a snack. “In India, they are mostly fed to cows,” she says. Alka points to ingredients like lulur, a wild amaranth used to make saag, and sohanjna (moringa) flowers used to make a raita, both of which became harder to come by in cities. Like many subcontinent cultures, tomatoes were never a part of Sindhi cuisine. Instead, souring agents like kokum jagul (monkey jackfruit), anardana (dried pomegranate), mithera (dried wild cucumber), gudamari (tamarind), katti palak (sorrel leaves), raw mango, yoghurt, kokum and lemon were used.

linked-story.headline: A spoonful, but with context: Why urban India is hungry for food history and science

story-elements.text: A spoonful, but with context: Why urban India is hungry for food history and science
Gradual loss of inheritance
The displacement reshaped everyday practices through which food traditions were passed down. Recipes that required time, patience, and specialised knowledge became harder to sustain.

Alka recalls a bread recipe followed by Sindhis living in the Punjab province of Multan that her husband’s grandmother often spoke about. Women gathered at tikanas (shrines) and shared fermented spiced water used to make doli ki roti, a fried stuffed roti. The roti comes with many stories. According to Alka’s grandmother-in-law, ‘doli’ refers to a container/earthen pot in which water was allowed to ferment and produce yeast (like a sourdough starter). Another belief suggests that because of its long shelf life, the roti was packed for brides travelling in a palanquin (doli) to be had on the way.

Another Multani delicacy is mukund wadi (seitan), made from wheat gluten. The dough is repeatedly washed to remove the starch, leaving behind an elastic gluten that is boiled and cut into pieces. Alka learnt the recipe from her elders and later discovered that they were also sold in some kirana stores.

story-elements.text: She also cites bheendi khatti, a raw mango pickle — a mixture of grated raw mango, mustard oil, peppercorns, nigella, fennel and fenugreek seeds, red chilli powder, asafoetida, jaggery and salt are placed in muslin potlis with a garlic pod in each of them. The potlis are immersed in vinaigrette, where, Alka explains, osmosis allows the flavours and juices to permeate the pickle.  Nishaste jo halwo was traditionally made by soaking and fermenting wheat for several days, then extracting, drying, and powdering its starch. Today, cornstarch is used. Praghree, traditionally made for Holi, is now mostly store-bought; “for Sindhis, Holi means ‘going crazy’ over sweets like praghree, gheeyar and malpura,” Alka writes in her blog, ‘Sindhi Rasoi’.
Survival and business

Food also became one of the ways Sindhis rebuilt their lives post-Partition. Pickles and papads were one of the first businesses to take off. Entrepreneurs built big brands like Chandu Halwai, Karachi Bakery, and Bhagat Tarachand.
Central to the post-Partition food movement was the dal pakhwan (spiced chana dal and crispy fried flatbread) street breakfast business, a comforting staple for the displaced community.

For Sindhis, ‘home’ is not just defined by geographical distance; it is also political. The generation that migrated remembered its markets, rivers and food. For the next generation, Sindh exists across a border that has become difficult to cross, even as it remains a place many ‘Indians’ call home. That is also the irony of “go to Pakistan” used as an insult today.
A song like ‘Daal chola dabal’ becomes worth returning to. It remembers Sindh through Radhe Mal, Moti Mal, street food and ordinary life — the things that make a place home.

headline: Small bites, big ideas: The rise of the amuse-bouche

seo.meta-description: Fine dining restaurants are elevating meals with creative amuse-bouche offerings, featuring bite-sized pre-appetisers that blend global flavours, local ingredients, and innovative culinary techniques to set the mood.
seo.meta-title: Amuse-bouche: Fine dining chefs redefine bite-sized appetisers in India

story.headline: Small bites, big ideas: The rise of the amuse-bouche

4a611db5-86b1-4865-a57a-608cd09a33e0.headline: Culinary trail across time zones: Food beyond the Ajanta-Ellora caves

story.subheadline: Fine dining spaces are getting creative with amuse-bouche or bite-sized offerings served as a prelude to a meal. From tartlets filled with creams and foams to spiced-up rose cookies and pani puris with a cocktail twist, small bites are making a big impact.
story.custom-slug: Small bites, big ideas: The rise of the amuse-bouche

story-elements.text: In one of the many hilarious episodes of ‘Friends’, Monica presents Chandler with an amuse-bouche (not commonly heard of in the 1990s), pronouncing it “amooze-boushe”, to which Chandler quips, “Well, it is amoooosing!”

Circa 2026, amuse-bouches sure are ‘amoosing’ diners across the city and the country. A French term that roughly translates to ‘mouth amuser’, an amuse-bouche refers to appetiser-like bites offered to diners before the main meal begins.

Dainty and often bite-sized, these pre-appetisers serve as a preview of the meal to come. “In addition to being a prelude, they help refresh and cleanse the palate, moving the guests away from what they had before entering the restaurant and preparing them for what to expect next,” explains Ridhi Choudhary, CEO, Mann & Salwa, which owns Vyanj, a progressive Indian cuisine restaurant in Ahmedabad. “At the same time, that one bite also gives you a glimpse of what the restaurant is all about,” she adds.
The restaurant experiments with familiar Indian ingredients to produce experiential textures and techniques.

Their amuse-bouche is a starfruit crème that brings together tangy mango jelly, light and refreshing starfruit shrikhand, charcoal boondi pearls and dehydrated starfruit. “In one bite, you get a sense of our approach to familiar Indian flavours presented through a different way of thinking,” notes Ridhi.
Evolution of the term

Although its exact origins are difficult to pinpoint, the term dates back to at least the mid-20th century, with ‘amuse-gueule’ being the earlier French expression (guele translates to mouth in French). The term, amuse-bouche, appeared in written French by the 1970s as the practice gained greater prominence with the rise of nouvelle cuisine, when chefs began favouring smaller, more inventive and visually refined preparations. By the 1980s, the amuse-bouche had become an increasingly familiar feature of fine dining, evolving into a way for chefs to offer diners a brief introduction to their culinary style even before the first course arrived.

Today, Indian chefs are getting increasingly creative with their amuse-bouches, offering a global fusion of flavours in a bite. From mini tartlets filled with creams and foams to spiced-up rose cookies and even pani puris with a cocktail twist, they use the quirky little bites to reflect the personality and philosophy of the space to the guests even before the dining experience begins.

linked-story.headline: Culinary trail across time zones: Food beyond the Ajanta-Ellora caves

story-elements.text: Culinary trail across time zones: Food beyond the Ajanta-Ellora caves

At Barnhouse, a vegetarian dining space at the retail and lifestyle destination Essensai067 in Whitefield, Bengaluru, the meal begins with a fruity start that captures the space’s farm-to-table philosophy. “The watermelon-based hors d’oeuvre highlights the freshness of the ingredient, topped with micro-herbs grown hydroponically and rich, creamy feta,” explains Siban Lal, head chef of the restaurant. With BarnHouse rooted in the concept of wellness, fresh produce and the philosophy of prana, the amuse-bouche follows the same principles, drawing on the contrast between freshness and richness while preparing the palate for what follows.
Dainty delights, big flavours
Another space that puts watermelon at the start of the dining experience is Heyou, the drinks-led bar and restaurant by Keen Mustard Ventures, Bengaluru.

True to its easy-going, cocktail-forward spirit, the venue infuses vodka into juicy watermelon chunks, giving guests a taste of what Heyou feels like even before the experience begins. “The dish sets the mood, builds anticipation, and captures the energy we want every guest to feel: vibrant, effortless, chilled out, and completely free of fuss,” observes Anirudh Kheny, co-founder of Heyou. “It is more than just a ritual. It is our way of saying, ‘Welcome to Heyou. This is the vibe.’”
Sakizuke love

With a growing love for Japanese cuisine in the city, sakizuke, the small opening courses traditionally served in Japanese dining, are also finding their way onto contemporary menus. At the recently-renovated UNO Izakaya at JW Marriott Hotel, Bengaluru, the concept emerged from several experiments with sushi rice.

“I started experimenting with the freshly prepared sushi rice that is sometimes left over at the end of the service rather than letting it go to waste. That led to our sushi rice cracker, served with a fermented chilli soy accompaniment, which eventually became the foundation of our sakizukes,” says Shubham Dhar, sous chef, UNO Izakaya. Today, the restaurant’s sakizuke evolves with different ingredients, textures, and seasons. From a light choux filled with celeriac cream and topped with tuna tartare and caviar to a tartlet with mango, scallop and ikura (salmon roe), each bite is designed to bring together contrasting flavours and textures.

“Whether it is vegetarian or non-vegetarian, the idea behind the sakizuke remains the same: to look at a familiar ingredient in a different way and create something unexpected. For me, that is what the sakizuke at UNO Izakaya represents. It is a small bite, but it tells you a lot about the kitchen.”

Be it in the form of a watermelon, star fruit or sushi rice, these bites are small in size but big on intent. Packed to deliver, they are a delicious way for chefs to introduce diners to their world of gastronomic wonders.

headline: A spoonful, but with context: Why urban India is hungry for food history and science

seo.meta-description: Cultural Insights: Urban Indian diners go beyond the plate, seeking history, culture, and context in every bite of native ingredients, artisan drinks, and traditional ferments.
seo.meta-title: Food Trends: Urban Indian diners go beyond the plate to taste food history

story.headline: A spoonful, but with context: Why urban India is hungry for food history and science
story.subheadline: A guava that tastes off, rice that smells of its soil, a pickle that makes one wonder about caste history: curiosity about food is taking urban Indian diners far beyond the plate. They are reading, tasting, questioning and discovering that every bite has its own backstory.
story.custom-slug: A spoonful, but with context: Why urban India is hungry for food history and science

story-elements.text: During the Covid lockdowns, Delhi-based Talish Ray noticed that the lauki (bottle gourd) and kaddu (pumpkin) she bought did not resemble the ones she recalled from childhood. “A Thai guava did not look, smell, or taste like the ones that I remembered,” she says. Her observations were not unusual; it’s just that she had the time to think about them then.

Ray, Advocate and Managing Partner at TRS Law Offices, had always been interested in food as a consumer and occasional cook. That curiosity, fuelled especially during the lockdown, led her to attend the first Indian Culinary Agenda (ICA) Weekend held in Delhi in 2024, an annual event of thematic talks and panel discussions by the Vrihi Foundation. An agri-food think tank positioned as a platform for India’s food researchers, writers and entrepreneurs, founder Om Routray says the aim is to turn “consumers into stakeholders for change”.
The curious diner

At this session, Ray found herself listening to policymakers, scientists, farmers and chefs discuss food from vantage points she had never considered. An entrepreneur spoke of efforts to bring native rice varieties back into cultivation. Supplementing that was a display of rice varieties gathered from across the country: Kala Namak from Siddharth Nagar in Uttar Pradesh, Chakhau, a black rice from Thoubal district in Manipur, and Jeeraga Samba from Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu, among others. Ray was hooked. “I remember thinking, finally I am in a space where people understand that rice, like water, can actually taste very different depending on the region,” she says.

story-elements.title: A 'Pop-up with a Purpose' session in progress in Bengaluru.

story-elements.text: The discussion around rice was immersive: how a staple most people think of only in terms of calories and nutrition could carry a distinct smell and texture, and even a different glycemic index, depending on where it was grown. Ray describes ICA as “food for the brain” and a kind of “university crash course”.

The change followed her home. She began sourcing rice from producers she had met at ICA and experimenting with mahua syrup in place of sugar. “It changed the pattern of consumption around our kitchen,” she says.

linked-story.headline: A gud deal

story-elements.text: A gud deal

Ray’s experience is part of a wider shift towards seeking knowledge in the food space. Knowing more about food has become part of the pleasure of eating it. People want to understand the drink in their glass, the fermentation behind a pickle, the history behind an ingredient or the social meanings attached to a meal.
Food is still the starting point, but the curious questions have taken a different turn.
What’s in the glass?

Take the questions around drinks. At The Good Craft Co. (TGCC) in Whitefield, Bengaluru, Vikram Damodaran, Chief Product Officer, DIAGEO India, has watched Indian consumers become far more discerning about what they drink over the past decade. “More importantly, they want to know more,” he says. “Why is one gin made differently from another? What does fermentation do to flavour? What is the story behind an indigenous spirit or ingredient?”

The Flavour Lab at TGCC began hosting consumer sessions in September 2024. Its four zones move participants through the process: an academy for spirit basics, R&D labs for experimentation, a fermentation wall on flavour development, and a bar where guided tastings bring it all together. These three-hour sessions are open to the public every Saturday.

story-elements.title: The fermentation wall at The Good Craft Co. in Whitefield, Bengaluru.

story-elements.text: The sessions are informal, comprising corporate professionals, artists, entrepreneurs and people from non-beverage industries. Participants smell botanicals, taste ingredients and hear from makers. One reaction comes up repeatedly, Damodaran says: “I never knew that went into my drink!”

There are only 14 seats in each session, and demand regularly outstrips them. Some return to contextualise their perspectives through different themes: gin and agave one month, whisky or indigenous spirits the next. That same appetite for context appears in food.
Through the lens of ferments
For Gurgaon-based Naheed Akhtar, Associate Director, Cultural Insights and Semiotics, Leapfrog Strategy Consulting, food has increasingly become a way of reading culture.

Akhtar began cooking and sourcing her own groceries from the mandi (the local wholesale market) in 2018, after moving from Bhubaneswar to Mumbai. Her interest grew through cooking with flatmates from different parts of the country, and her work as a semiotician gave her another way of looking at it.

She encountered Desi Cultures, an initiative that explores the diversity of traditional Indian fermented foods and practices, through an Instagram story by Shivani Unakar, the festival’s food systems researcher, facilitator and producer. Fermentation, Akhtar discovered, wasn’t simply about preserving food or flavour: it opened into questions of people, place, history and power.

At Fermenty Cultures, an offsite event in Lucknow during this year’s Desi Cultures festival, Akhtar encountered foods such as khamiri roti (fermented wheat bread) with tale gosht (mutton) and aloo ka salan, gulgule, a sweet fritter made from leftover fermented wheat dough, and nabidh (fermented date drink). She also found newer fermentation businesses experimenting with turning SCOBY (the bacteria-and-yeast culture used to ferment kombucha) into organic leather.

The initiative’s online sessions explored the politics of fermentation, its pedagogy, food justice and its archaeology. Akhtar found herself thinking about how ideas of ‘clean’ and ‘unclean’ food can be shaped by caste, class, gender, modernity and imperialism. One example stayed with her: a hierarchy in the Manusmriti that considered fermented dairy clean but fermented meat unclean, which made her think about who decides what is permissible, and what is edible.

She also found herself focusing on the labour embedded in food and how the microbes on our own hands can influence taste. Fermentation, in other words, became a way of seeing. Akhtar now has at least one fermented food most days, whether pickle or curd, and is considering making kombucha, a ginger bug and kanji. But the more interesting change is conceptual. “I see food as a lens through which we can understand changing consumer values, aspirations and ways of living,” she says, “through sustainability, healing, authenticity, convenience and the reinterpretation of tradition.”

From a three-day virtual seminar organised by food researcher and filmmaker Shubhra Chatterji during the pandemic, Desi Cultures, in its 2026 edition, has grown into more than 25 independent satellite events across 12 cities, hosted by anyone who wanted to celebrate desi ferments in their own way, from workshops and tastings to panels and story circles. With 340 registered participants this year, from all over India, including people from 23 different countries, Unakar says the response showed that people were hungry not just to learn, but to gather and share their ‘nerdiness’ about fermentation. That appetite for learning is not restricted to just things that can be tasted.
Food and words
Pankhuri Agrawal, Founder at Yayavr Food Readers’ Club in Bengaluru, approaches food through another route: reading.

On May 6, 2023, Yayavr held its first Beginners Online class on how to pre-read non-fiction books on food. Limited to 15 participants and run more like a seminar than a lecture, it filled within three hours. Participants worked through Robin Wall Kimmerer’s Braiding Sweetgrass, letting its imagery surface their own childhood memories of gardens, then moved on to Sundar Sarukkai’s Philosophy for Children and its idea that critical reading is really “about choosing and connecting what we choose” to read.

The idea, for Agrawal, came from watching people struggle with critical reading. While culinary resources were plentiful, Agrawal felt that the academic side of food remained out of reach for those outside formal research environments. Twelve such workshops have followed since.

The age of participants has ranged from 20 to 65 years, with people signing in from across India and internationally, including Hanoi, London, Atlanta, and parts of the US. The profile ranges from archivists and chefs to journalists, academics, lawyers and homemakers. Young mothers, often excluded from in-person sessions due to travel time and family commitments, are able to attend as well.

At her Food Readers’ Club, participants take an ingredient, a dish, a beverage or a concept  — sugar, salt, toddy, filter coffee, chai, funeral food — and place it alongside literary, journalistic, sociological, anthropological or historical writing. A discussion around salt brought attention to labour. A tea session reframed it as a plantation product, and the workers’ rights that follow from that label. A discussion on disgust made people notice their office’s separate microwaves for vegetarian and meat food.
“The Food Readers’ Club has definitely changed the way members eat and order food,” Agrawal says. “We have all become more cognisant of the layers of history, culture and society that food carries.”
That may be the simplest reason this kind of learning appeals: the curiosity doesn’t end when the session does. It follows people back into ordinary life.
Know your next choice

For Bengaluru-based Foodwize co-founders Priya Joshi and Srijata Sengupta, that movement from knowledge to everyday decision-making is central to what they do. Their work spans multiple formats. Pop-Up with a Purpose focuses on tasting and conversation around buying food wisely; Wize Plate is a multisensory take on Indian food for workplaces; and STHIRA is a national student innovation challenge.

“Young people interested in the future of the planet want to address problems they see. The students of Sustainable Development at XIM Bhubaneshwar created a portable torch of kilos of fruit waste to help a juice vendor deal with the lack of electricity in the evenings. Civil engineering students of Alliance University, Bengaluru, designed a green roof with edible leaves to grow food on top of urban buildings. Students of Bhanuben Nanavati College of Architecture, Pune, ideated on how to grow food in parts of scrapped cars,” explain Joshi and Sengupta, adding that STHIRA has reached students across 45+ universities, 400+ colleges and 125+ cities and 18 disciplines.

Since Foodwize began three years ago, over 2,000 people have attended their consumer programmes. The audience is not defined simply by being ‘foodies’. It includes people at points of transition in their lives: new mothers, parents of teenagers, working professionals, young couples and teachers, who are increasingly thinking differently about food. After a few Wize Plate sessions, participants told the founders they had begun teaching what they had learned to their own children. “It is a sign that our approach is not only helping the individual,” Joshi and Sengupta say, “it is making them feel confident about equipping others to eat well.”
Sustainability is not a sacrifice but a higher-return decision, they say, and all Foodwize experiences are designed for people to realise this opportunity.
Shifting ideas

It’s a common pattern: curiosity is enjoyable on its own, but it also shapes the choices people make afterwards. Foodwize’s participants say it has changed how they shop. Agrawal’s readers order their meals differently. The changes also show up in people’s own work, as a new angle on an existing one. Ray hopes to work in geographical indications (GI), the tags that protect regional produce, in the near future, a direction she traces straight back to ICA. She would also like to see the event itself grow bigger: longer, more immersive, opened up to schools and law colleges.

Akhtar draws a similar connection through her own lens: fermentation tells her something about shifting ideas of sustainability and authenticity. What she wants more of isn’t discussion but doing: workshops, field visits, tastings.

Today’s curiosity isn’t just about the next trending restaurant, or the newest bar to try. It isn’t even about the storytelling that such spaces offer with their food and drink, curated as it often is. This kind of learning and exploration is driven organically, and thus makes the discoveries more personal and satisfying. It lets people answer questions they didn’t know they had, drawn from their own experience and exposure, and find more rabbit holes to go down into. As Damodaran puts it, once people open one door, there are ten others to explore.

story.subheadline: Aurangabad, now Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, offers an array of gastronomic choices. From curated organic meals to exciting street eats, food has begun to shape the way you experience the city.
story.custom-slug: Culinary trail across time zones: Food beyond the Ajanta-Ellora caves

story-elements.text: To me, the UNESCO-heritage sites of the Ajanta and Ellora mountain caves in Maharashtra’s Aurangabad, now Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar, have always been those black and white pictures that formed part of our history textbooks in school. Recently, I visited the caves for the first time.

Nothing prepared me for what my mind took a good half hour to comprehend. The Ajanta and Ellora caves are hand-carved from top down and then breadth-wise. It took at least two generations of artisans to complete one cave, which means that none of the artisans nor the kings who funded them ever saw their work complete. These caves were created for the future — for Buddhist monks who needed a place to rest, for travellers seeking refuge, and for locals who came seeking spiritual guidance.

Centuries later, as scores of people wander through these well-preserved caves, the wonder of their creation never ceases. Walking through them, and on the way out, the first thing that hits you is hunger. Not just the usual kind, but something sharper. (Possibly because your brain is still trying to process what it just saw.)

With improved connectivity, easier access to the caves, and a growing range of places to stay, Aurangabad is finding its way onto travel circuits. And along the way, food begins to shape the experience in ways you don’t quite plan for.

story-elements.text: About half an hour from Ellora, Dhyaana Farms makes a strong case for being more than just a place to check into. This five-room farm stay sits within a working organic farm, where meals are central to the experience rather than an add-on. “It’s not a conventional restaurant setup,” says Sahaj Sharma, co-owner. “Meals are curated rather than ordered.”

The dining space sets the tone immediately — a glass-enclosed living room placed in the middle of the farm, where meals unfold at an unhurried pace. “Daily harvests directly influence what goes on the plate,” Sharma says, and that translates into menus that shift constantly.
From Maharashtrian to European

A meal might begin with a traditional Maharashtrian thali — seasonal vegetables, lentils, local breads — and move into Mediterranean and European plates built around grilled meats, roasted vegetables, and fresh salads made with in-house greens. The transitions feel natural, less like a menu switch and more like a continuation of the same idea.

There’s also an in-house bakery that anchors everything. Multigrain breads and sourdough come out warm, paired with seasonal preserves — strawberry, apple, pineapple — made on the property. And just when you think you are done, out come the ragi-based cookies, gluten-free bakes, and simple tea cakes that your tummy miraculously makes place for.

In the city, Accentuate Food Lab offers a completely different kind of meal. Chef Mohib Farooqui runs an eight-seater tasting menu space that feels almost improbable in a city like Aurangabad. It began as something small— initially not even intended for diners, but for friends — and has since evolved into a space built on conviction rather than scale.

Menus change every few months, moving between nine and thirteen courses, each built around a theme. Some of these themes have been Italian, North African, and Dakhani. There’s a noticeable restraint in how the food is presented and explained. The focus is less on technical display and more on how the diner experiences each course in the moment.

Alongside the tasting menus, there’s also a Levantine family-style meal, shaped by Farooqui’s childhood in the Middle East. In a city so strongly defined by its past, this feels like a different kind of narrative entering the table.
And everything in between...

At Hira Pao Bhaji, the pao bhaji is heavy on butter, and the pao is toasted just enough to soak it all in. At Mathura Wala, soft dahi bhallas come layered with sweet and tangy chutneys that lean fully into indulgence. Meals tend to end at one of the city’s paan counters — Tara Paan Centre or Aurangabad Paan Centre — where the ritual feels as important as the paan itself.

For something more substantial, Jama Khan Mandi serves large-format mandi — aromatic rice with meat, built for sharing — while Mustafa Biryani delivers the kind of slow-cooked, spice-layered biryani that locals return to often. Dhyaana Farms curates special sit-down mandi dining experiences, allowing guests to enjoy a similar communal feast in a more immersive, curated setting. You don’t arrive in Aurangabad expecting to map it through food. But between caves, curated meals, and street-side stops, that’s exactly what ends up happening.

Famous five

Some of the most popular dishes that the city is famous for, thanks to food influences from the Delhi Sultanate, Mughal, Maratha, Deccan, and Nizam era include:

Naan qalia/khaliya: Meat slow cooked and infused with yoghurt and a range of ingredients including poppy seeds, chironji, and desiccated coconut, among others. This is eat with naan.

Aurangabad kantakki: A take on KFC (fried chicken), and is a big hit in the city. Crunchy pieces of chicken are also mixed with rice.

Tikiya pao: A tikiya (patty) made of minced meat and spices and wedged in between a bun makes for tikiya pao.

Samosa rice: Crushed samosas with potato stuffing, mixed with rice and spicy gravy.

Imarti: A deep-fried sweet delicacy made of urad dal batter and dipped in sugar syrup.

story-elements.text: Call it kadubu in Kannada, kudumu in Telugu, kozhukatta/kozhukattai in Tamil Nadu and Keralam, modaks across Maharashtra and other parts of India, the sweet dumpling is an invariable part of a festive meal, especially during Ganesha Chaturthi. In Goa, Mangaluru and parts of coastal Karnataka, the fried version is called neureo or nevri and is made during festivals like Deepavali, Ganesh Chaturthi, and Christmas. From jackfruit stuffing to modern-day fillings made of dates, chocolate and rose flavours, the dish has lent itself to creativity rather well. The sometimes-steamed, sometimes-deep fried delicacy comes with a rice or wheat wrapper while the traditional stuffings use a combination of lentil, jaggery, and coconut.

The word modaka is derived from the Sanskrit moda-ka, meaning that which delights. Food historian K T Achaya, in the book, Indian food: a historical companion, traces the evolution of the modaka and “madhugõlaka” (literally honeyed globes) through the emergence of guda ( jaggery) which replaced honey during the Buddhist period. Honey was predominantly used in the Vedic period. Manasollasa, the work of 12th-century Chalukyan King Someshwara III also cites the modaka, and says the sweet was called varshopalagolakas or hailstones. Ancient medical practitioners (Charaka, Sushrutha and Vaghbhata) used the word modaka to describe a sweet uncooked pill, writes Achaya.

story-elements.text: No theft of 'modak' from Puri Jagannath temple: Minister
Beyond India

Dumplings are not the preserve of India alone. From the East European pierogi with sweet fillings, to China’s tangyuan (sweet rice balls) that marked their festivities and the Japanese kangidan, they are a part of the food tradition in most regions of the world. While there is no single origin story around the dumpling, as Barbara Gallani in her book, Dumplings: A Global History, says the dish has developed “independently in different parts of the world through the use of common ingredients. Travel and commercial exchanges have contributed to the transfer of certain shapes and combinations of tastes from country to country and across continents.”

headline: Oxford study warns people sipping 'piping hot' chai of esophageal cancer

seo.meta-title: Oxford study warns people sipping 'piping hot' chai of esophageal cancer
seo.meta-description: A major Oxford University study reveals drinking tea or coffee at temperatures above 65°C may triple the risk of oesophageal cancer. The research, tracking over a million adults, highlights how repeated thermal injury to the food pipe increases cancer risk.

story.headline: Oxford study warns people sipping 'piping hot' chai of esophageal cancer

7cd76f88-109c-4f2e-866c-ed0bde3ca3c5.headline: Two to three cups of 'chai' every day can be therapeutic, study finds

story.subheadline: A major English study has found that a common practice of drinking tea at boiling temperatures may be silently increasing one’s risk of esophageal cancer.

story-elements.text:
The first thing India reaches for after waking up from slumber is a hot, brewing cup of chai or coffee.

While focus has been primarily on the caffeine content or the adequate number of cups in a day, rarely people have stopped to ask at what temperature must they take the first sip.

“I prefer drinking tea hot enough not to burn my tongue,” said a user on Reddit.

Another joined the chat and said: “I feel the flavors more strongly at room temperature for some reason.”

When Local Circles survey asked a sample crowd on their preferred caffeine drink, about 69 per cent surveyed people voted for tea and the other 26 per cent turned out to be coffee fans.

After years of repeatedly sipping these caffeine boosters, a major English study, coming from researchers at Oxford University, has found that a common practice of drinking them at boiling temperatures may be silently increasing one’s risk of esophageal cancer.

linked-story.headline: Two to three cups of 'chai' every day can be therapeutic, study finds

story-elements.text: Two to three cups of 'chai' every day can be therapeutic, study finds

Tea boils at and above 100 degree C

The large scale study published in the journal International Journal of Cancer which has analyzed about one million adults from the UK, said any drink above 65 degrees Celsius poses a potential risk of causing cellular damage and increases risk of cancer.

Tea brewing on a stove usually boils at 100 degrees Celsius, around the same temperature as that of water. 

When one pours it into the mug, the temperature may fall down to a bearable 80 or 90 degree Celsius.

However, it may still not be at an optimum temperature for consumption, the study stated, even if one adds milk to it, which may cool it down a bit.

While some wait for the drink to get at its room temperature, others may promptly sip.

In a typical Indian household with standard ventilation, the average room temperature should usually range between 20 degrees C and 28 degrees C.

What did the study find?

The study looked at adults from two major cohort studies, Million Women Study and UK Biobank. The number of participants was around 1 million in a rough sum.

They followed the participants for around 11 to 14 years, and zoomed in particularly on two kinds of esophageal cancer, squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma (AC).

Finding a link between drink temperature and esophageal cancer, the researchers said that people who consumed tea or coffee at very high temperatures (above 65 degrees C) had three times more risk of developing esophageal cancer than those who drank it at moderate or ‘warm temperatures.’

Among the types, the risk was three times higher for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), the layer of tissues lining the food pipe, and negligible for adenocarcinoma (AC) (mostly develops in the glandular cells).

As per experts, repeated thermal injury in the esophageal lining may increase the risk of cellular mutations.

Frequency also matters

According to the study, the temperature of the drink alone does not increase the cancer risk but also the frequency of ‘very hot’ drinks.

It found that people who consumed over 6 cups of piping hot drinks had 71 per cent higher risk of esophageal SCC than those drinking less.

Hence, the number of hot drinks also counts.

Difficult to fix a temperature

As per researchers, the 65 degrees Celsius is just a makeshift standard as it is hard to quantify a suitable temperature to consume a drink.

In other words, what may be ‘too hot’ for one person may be perceived as ‘warm’ by another. Since sensation is also a subjective experience, it is hard to find a number that fits all. 

Hence, more research is needed in this direction to quantify the established link.

Do it the Indian ‘tapri’ way!

It is common to see tea vendors transferring tea from one container to another at the nearest ‘tapri’.

While there are multiple explanations to it, including frequently dispersing the crowd around tea stalls or to bring out the milky froth, the act also works out well in bringing down the temperature of chai, bringing the stimulating drink at moderate temperature.

So, next time you sit with your tea, make sure it gets a break to cool down!

headline: Before Biryani, there was Khichadi: The ancient story of India’s one-pot meals

seo.meta-description: One-Pot Recipes: Delve into the history and evolution of single-pot meals like khichadi, tehari, and biryani. From ancient grains to rich flavours, these dishes blend tradition with convenience, offering unique tastes and nutritious choices.

story.subheadline: From simple rice and lentil dishes to pulao, tehari and the layered biryani, one-pot meals are nutrition-rich, convenient and flavourful. Zubin D'Souza writes about the layered history of one pot meals, some of which appear in ancient texts
story.custom-slug: Before Biryani, there was Khichadi: The ancient story of India’s one-pot meals

story-elements.text: The origins of one-pot meals actually lie more in frugality as compared to practicality. Cooking utensils were not cheap and neither was firewood always plentiful. There was the added disadvantage of not being allowed the use of multiple stoves. So, one-pot meals started becoming the norm. And why shouldn’t they be? They are nutritious because all the water-soluble vitamins and minerals remain inside the pot. They are convenient to prepare, consume and clean up afterwards. And I think that the biggest advantage has to be that the intermingling of flavours within the confined space makes the resultant dish so much more delicious.

linked-story.headline: Good biryani spot in Japan? Relishing Indian food in Tokyo and beyond

story-elements.text: Good biryani spot in Japan? Relishing Indian food in Tokyo and beyond

Single pot-style food recipes have appeared in ancient texts and treatises. They have gone by various names and have had a thrilling trajectory in terms of ingredients used and combinations experimented upon. From the mudga khichadi that graced Vedic literature to the oon sooru that made its appearance in Tamil poetry from the Sangam era in the first century CE, we have had a strong affinity to rice all through our evolution. So much so that we even believe rice to be connected to the divine. It is part of our rituals and nods to the gods while also staying a source of sustenance throughout our lives.

linked-story.headline: Good biryani spot in Japan? Relishing Indian food in Tokyo and beyond

story-elements.text: Good biryani spot in Japan? Relishing Indian food in Tokyo and beyond

The khichadi is by far the oldest, with references being found in the ancient Indian medical traditions of Ayurveda. It has a recurring theme throughout our history. It is a single-pot rice and lentil dish that was used as an invigorative for patients who were recovering from illnesses. It was traditionally a simple farmworker meal. The term is believed to have evolved as a result of an amalgamation of two very distinct Sanskrit terms, keech and anna, which essentially mean rice and lentils. The evolution of khichadi has been a long and arduous process, and there are now multiple options to the lentils used or spices involved. The lentils used varied on the occasion. Mung dal for patients, arhar dal for celebrations, chana dal for texture and whole urad dal for nostalgia. A biryani is a far richer and complex dish. It involves spices, copious amounts of ghee or butter and is always prepared for ceremonial and celebratory occasions.
Biryani & its versions

Technically, a biryani, under most circumstances, is not a one-pot meal. Biryanis usually have the rice and the primary protein cooked separately and then combined in a single pot for the final preparation. A biryani may be a mélange or could have the rice and meats in layers. Biryanis over time have developed their own regional identities which in many cases may only have the type of rice used swapped for one of another variety. Now, tehari was often thought to be made as a consolation for those vegetarians who could not eat biryanis. But a tehari seems to have a much older origin story than that. A tehari is a classic single-pot meal that usually combines rice with vegetables. These are predominantly carbohydrate-and fibre-rich meals that were designed to give a burst of energy to the diner.

linked-story.headline: Kerala consumer forum orders biryani outlet to pay Rs 96,500 to woman over contaminated food

story-elements.text: Kerala consumer forum orders biryani outlet to pay Rs 96,500 to woman over contaminated food
Easy to digest

A tehari usually does not contain lentils or any such protein and is meant to be easily digestible. A tehari ends up with the rice clumping together in most cases because of the reduced amounts of fat being used. This is in line with its primary objective of traditionally being a frugal meal. In many cases, a tehari would shun the use of onions and garlic as flavourings in a subtle nod to their origins and popularity amongst followers of the Jain religion. In a similar vein, they also may not use root vegetables and be flavoured with asafoetida to replace the flavour that one could obtain from onion and garlic.
After the advent of biryanis and the introduction of pulao to the Indian culinary repertoire, tehari has undergone a minor shift.

There are now two versions of tehari that are acceptable. The new version emerged from the modern-day state of Uttar Pradesh, where a tehari can also be khulla. Khulla, which means open, is a reference to following the recipe and technique that ensures that the grains do not stick to each other.

A pulao, also called pulav, pilaf, pollo and pilao depending on which part of the country you hail from, walks a different path. It too is a ceremonial and festive rice preparation that is very often cooked in stock and with mild spices. The rice grains in a pulao need to be separate and that is exactly what determines the skill level of the chef.
(Excerpted with permission from the book, A Quest for the Perfect Rice, published by Penguin Random House India.)
