39337657-33d1-444e-9535-fcf40fccf07a.headline: World Biryani Day: This city in India is known as 'Biryani Capital'—can you guess it?

story.subheadline: Across Tokyo and beyond, specialist biryani kitchens are mushrooming, established South Asian restaurants are expanding their offerings.
story.custom-slug: biryani-oishii-says-japan

story-elements.text: “Honestly, I never expected biryani in Tokyo to be that good,” says Priya Somani, still raving about a plate she recently relished in the Japanese capital. The Bengaluru-based software engineer who was visiting the country last month had gone in with modest expectations. What she encountered instead was “fragrant rice, tender meat and spices that unfolded slowly, layer after layer”, leaving her surprised that a dish so deeply associated with India could feel so compelling thousands of kilometers away.

The enthusiasm is increasingly reciprocal. Recently, Japanese Ambassador to India Ono Keiichi shared a photograph from his visit to Telangana, where he ate authentic Hyderabadi biryani. His post was another sign of how the dish is travelling between the two countries.

In Tokyo and other Japanese cities, specialist restaurants are drawing diners curious to explore the dish. Chef Takamasa Osawa of the ten-seat Biriyani Osawa, which recently bagged the prestigious Michelin Bib Gourmand (given globally to restaurants delivering value-for-money meals), has taken his fascination with the dish to the next level. He regularly does pop-ups in India creating a two-way culinary conversation. Osawa’s restaurant serves virtually nothing but biryani. He says he discovered the dish while travelling in India and spent years exploring its regional variations and considering how it could evolve in Japan.

story-elements.title: Chef Takamasa Osawa. Pic courtesy: Biriyani Osawa

linked-story.headline: World Biryani Day: This city in India is known as 'Biryani Capital'—can you guess it?

story-elements.text: World Biryani Day: This city in India is known as 'Biryani Capital'—can you guess it?
Fragrance at the core

“Biryani can evolve even further,” he says, viewing it not as a fixed recipe but as a technique with the potential to absorb different ingredients and culinary influences. His approach is particularly informed by the meeting point between Indian and Japanese tastes. “If Indian cuisine were a band, the aroma would be the lead singer,” he says, reflecting his belief that fragrance is central to the biryani experience.

Across Tokyo and beyond, specialist biryani kitchens are mushrooming, established South Asian restaurants are expanding their offerings, and diners are learning to distinguish between regional styles — from Hyderabadi and Kolkata biryani to versions shaped by the culinary traditions of South India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.

Tokyo-based restaurants such as Erick South, Dakshin, Nirvanam, and Torkari have broadened Japanese diners’ understanding of the diversity of Indian and South Asian cooking. Torkari offers biryani in many forms, including mutton, chicken, fish, and prawn. “The rise is particularly striking in a country where rice is not simply a staple but a subject of culinary obsession. Japanese cuisine has elevated rice through sushi, donburi and countless regional preparations,” explains Torkari’s Chef Yuji Uno. Biryani introduces an entirely different philosophy: long-grained basmati layered with meat, spices, herbs and aromatics, cooked such that each grain remains separate while carrying the flavours of everything beneath it, Uno adds.
Beyond naan & curry

For decades, Indian food in Japan meant curry, naan, and tandoori chicken. That is changing, say local Japanese chefs and travellers. The biryani is now capturing the imagination of Japanese diners. “For me, the biryani’s appeal lies in the fact that it’s not a one-note meal. Relishing the fragrance of cardamom or cloves, the richness of the meat, followed by the heat of chilli or the sweetness of caramelised onions makes the dish so soulful,” explains Delhi-based expat Akihiro Sato, who often orders biryani at home.

Chefs are now eyeing Japan’s seafood, vegetables, and seasonal produce, which offer new possibilities with the biryani. Says Osawa, “I want to turn all the ingredients in the supermarket into biryani.” This fervour marks a fascinating cultural exchange: reinterpretations of the dish being lapped up in both countries.

headline: Food for comfort: How traditions shape our cravings and mindful eating choices

seo.meta-description: Mindful eating: Comfort food can reflect family traditions, culture and personal identity. From rasam-rice and dal to global favourites, thoughtful food choices can support gut health, mindful habits and a more sustainable relationship with what we eat.
seo.meta-title: Food for comfort: How traditions shape our cravings and mindful eating choices

story.headline: Food for comfort: How traditions shape our cravings and mindful eating choices
story.subheadline: The idea that food is meaningful and significant in the fight to restore planetary health is quite integral in the broader narrative of holistic wellness today.

story-elements.text:
My daughter had caught a stomach bug for a few days, and lost her appetite. Once the fever had let up, she was craving something slightly savoury and spicy to revive her palate. “Rasam, rice and potatoes on the side,” she said, “that’s comfort food for me, especially when I’m under the weather.”

Having been through an array of comfort food choices across different ages and the continents we traversed during those growing up years, this came as a pleasant surprise to me. No more pasta with pink sauce, I thought to myself, or PB&Js (peanut butter and jelly/jam sandwiches). She added a couple of other things to the list, like rajma-chawal with pickled onions and rice with thick, yellow dal, mixed with ghee.

While all of these things are reflective of the multi-cuisine culture in my kitchen, it got me thinking about how traditions affect our yearning for comfort food. My childhood was pivoted around food from Malnad and Kolar, where my maternal and paternal grandparents were from, respectively: think pickles and kadubus. This brought back something I’d read in grad school: food and nutrition expert Annie Hauck-Lawson’s description of “food voice,” where food is a “channel for the expression of meaning.” I grew up being encouraged to hear food as a voice and over the years, I’ve learned to recognise the subtler details in my food, its dialects and inflections and the idea of personal identity that stems from it.

Mixed bag of culinary traditions

My travels and inter-cultural marriage are the two big factors that decreed the kind of cook I’d become, and the culture of my kitchen. My daughter grew up on a staple diet of delicacies from this curious mixed bag of culinary traditions, covering everything from rasam-rice to aloo-sheddho-bhaat, with mac-and-cheese, deep dish pizzas and pavlovas and golden kiwi topped with hokey pokey ice cream, from across the world, thrown in for good measure.

One common thread in all these variables has always been: mindful eating. I’ve always encouraged her to reflect on what she’s eating, to forge a deeper connection with the food as well as its broader impact on the planet. This isn’t something to brag about, of course — the idea that food is meaningful and significant in the fight to restore planetary health is quite integral in the broader narrative of holistic wellness today.

Like anthropologist Sidney Mintz said, "For us humans eating is never a 'purely biological' activity. The foods eaten have histories associated with the pasts of those who eat them; the techniques employed to find, process, prepare, serve, and consume the foods are all culturally variable, with histories of their own.

Here are some tips to stay rooted in awareness and comfort as you think about meal-planning
and grocery shopping for you and your family:

• Listen to your body's cues. Being attuned to your hunger signals and knowing when you are satisfied (as opposed to overfull) can guide you towards making healthier choices, especially better portion control without the added onus of guilt.

• Identifying triggers that lead to stress eating is important — by getting a grip on your eating patterns, you will be better equipped to build healthier habits and a more conscious approach to eating.

• Rather than thinking of a meal in its entirety, delve into the ingredients you choose: what’s their origin, what stories are linked to them in the farmer community and in socio-cultural contexts? This approach helps you acknowledge the journey of the ingredients from the earth to a food on your plate, helping you understand everything from nutritional value to resource intensity.

• Don’t think about food as nourishment alone: it is not a unilateral case in point. Your mood dictates what and how you eat, and the reverse is true as well. What you eat (and how it’s prepared) affects how you feel. Learn to choose foods that make you feel grounded and are easy on your gut. The easiest way to do this is to visit your local market, have conversations with the vendors and understand local produce and the
traditional ways in which they’re cooked. No matter where you are, commit to eating what’s grown around you and take responsibility for the choices you make.

• Every meal presents an opportunity for reflection and intention. Learn to build simple habits at the table, which foster a sense of gratitude and appreciation for the foods you choose to cook and eat. As you navigate the intricacies of your health goals, remember to consider the entire ecosystem that helps put food on your table.

(Ranjini is a communications professor, author, and podcaster, straddling many other worlds, in Bengaluru. She’s passionate about urban farming and sustainable living, and can mostly be found cooking and baking in her little kitchen, where, surrounded by heirloom coffee kettles and mismatched tea cups, she finds her chi.)

headline: Sweet, spice and history: Exploring layered flavors of Moroccan cuisine

seo.meta-description: Moroccan cuisine: From tagine and couscous to pastilla and mint tea, Morocco's food reflects Amazigh, Arab, Jewish, Andalusian and Mediterranean influences, blending sweet, savoury and spicy flavours with a rich culture of hospitality.
seo.meta-title: Sweet, spice and history: Exploring layered flavors of Moroccan cuisine

story.headline: Sweet, spice and history: Exploring layered flavors of Moroccan cuisine
story.subheadline: Moroccan cuisine is a delicious mix of many influences, from Amazigh and Andalusian to Mediterranean and African. Rashmi Vasudeva samples an array of dishes and is taken in by the contrasts on offer — meat with prunes, savoury and sweet pastilla, and refreshing mint tea.

story-elements.text:
It is more than a little disconcerting when effusive travel-brochure declarations turn out to be true. Every time you read about Morocco, there’s that sentence: a country of contrasts. At least in its cuisine, I discovered it certainly is. Meat arrives with prunes; a slow-cooked beef stew can taste fruity and spicy, with a hint of floral; desserts have orange blossoms adorning them; and, oh, figs and almonds appear when you least expect them, sometimes sitting pretty next to lemon zest in a meat dish. This is a cuisine that seems to have absorbed Morocco itself: Amazigh, Andalusian, Arab, Jewish, Mediterranean, and African influences all merge in a country that’s always trying to do several things at once.

It took me a while to understand that this is not Moroccans being random. Moroccan food is a repository of all the people who have passed through this land. The Amazigh (the indigenous people of North Africa) influence runs deep; Arab traditions, as well as the cuisines of Muslim and Jewish communities, and influences from Spain and other Mediterranean countries, have all found their way into Moroccan kitchens.

Tagine experience

The first dish most visitors meet is, inevitably, the tagine. I had seen the familiar conical pot countless times, but watching one emerge from a kitchen with such ceremony is an experience by itself.

The vessel is both cooking pot and serving dish, its distinctive lid designed to return condensed steam to the food. The result? Slow-cooked meat, be it beef or chicken, is never chewy or hard. Saturated with spice and sauces, it is meat that melts. The combinations are creative. You will find chicken paired with olives, with an occasional fig peeping out. Lamb may arrive alongside prunes and apricots or even vegetables. This renders nearly every dish a permutation of sweet and spice.

Then there is the couscous, which is quite literally everywhere. An acquired taste at best, or so was my impression. That was because, before I visited Morocco, all I had seen of couscous was unappetising mounds in some fine-dining restaurants. Here, it is not only the national dish, but you also find Moroccans actually being affectionate towards it. While couscous is basically semolina rolled till fluffy and steamed, it is the topping that matters: often a combination of vegetables, meat and dried fruits that are available aplenty in the country.

Time for a ‘dessert’

In Fez, I got to savour the most startling sweet-savoury ‘dessert’ of them all: the pastilla. Get this: It looks like a pastry with a filling. Now, it has almond shavings on top (usually) and is essentially a pie with crisp, thin layers of pastry with a filling of, err... shredded chicken or shrimp (yes), sometimes fish, traditionally rabbit or pigeon meat. It is slow-cooked (yes, this too) with spices such as cinnamon, ginger and saffron, and the final flourish is the dusting of powdered sugar on top. Sounds improbable? But, weirdly enough, it makes sense. For you see, Fez was a town that several communities passed through, often in long caravans on their way to the Strait of Gibraltar. Recipes, cooking techniques and taste all were fused to produce something as curious as the pastilla.

Once you leave the urban splendour behind and drive towards the Sahara, the food gets earthier. The Amazigh influence becomes particularly visible, and the focus is on food that doesn’t weigh your tummy down but gives you energy. Think dates, almonds, olives, and flatbreads. The Medfouna, for instance, is a stuffed flatbread packed with minced meat, herbs and spices. In the desert’s sand and heat, food becomes both restoration and an experience. You end up eating light, but you also pay it more obeisance.
Whisky, err...tea

Moroccans have a standard running joke: that they consume ‘whisky’ at all times of the day. This ‘whisky’ is, of course, the famous Moroccan mint tea. The story goes that the greater the height from which it is poured, the greater the love you will receive. From whom, I asked, and one particularly genial Moroccan told me it could be from the one you have always loved, the one who has always loved you, the universe, or God... take your pick. Tea, sugar (Moroccans get mildly offended if you take your mint tea without sugar), and mint may be simple ingredients, but Moroccan mint tea is not really about the tea itself. It is about the country’s culture of hospitality: tea is an excuse to welcome you, chat with you, and its pouring is a little performance designed to convince you to stay.
(The writer was in Morocco recently at the invitation of the Moroccan National Tourist Office.)

story.subheadline: Swatee Jog shares four easy-to-make mocktail recipes featuring jamun, mango, blueberry and green apple to keep your celebrations bubbling with flavour.

story-elements.text:
The festive season gives you the perfect reason to host sundowner parties with family and friends. The menu may be elaborate, with Indian dinner staples piling up on the table. But your mocktails can bring a refreshing burst of flavour and colour.

A perfect mocktail balances four elements: sweetness, acidity, aroma, and fizz. Fruit purees lend body, a dash of citrus adds contrast, herbs and spices bring complexity, and soda provides that celebratory sparkle. Floral notes such as rose and hibiscus add elegance, while ingredients such as ginger, black pepper, and cardamom keep the drinks from becoming cloyingly sweet.

Here are a few festive recipes. Serve them in wine glasses, coupe glasses, tall tumblers, or traditional brass glasses for a festive touch.

Jamun, Rosemary and Lime Blast

Jamun makes for a dramatic-looking mocktail, while rosemary contributes a woody, pine-like aroma that contrasts beautifully with the fruit’s natural tartness. Lime and soda keep everything lively.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 2 cups ripe jamun, deseeded and pureed, or 1 cup canned jamun juice

— 60 ml fresh lime juice

— 60 ml sugar syrup, or to taste

— 4 small sprigs of fresh rosemary

— 600 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— Thin lime wheels, for garnish

— 4 small rosemary sprigs, for serving

Method

— Blend the jamun puree with the lime juice and sugar syrup until smooth.

— Lightly bruise four small rosemary sprigs between your fingers to release their aroma. Add them to the jamun mixture and leave to infuse for five minutes. Remove the sprigs.

— Divide the mixture equally among four ice-filled glasses.

— Top each glass with approximately 150 ml of chilled soda and stir gently.

— Garnish with a lime wheel and a fresh rosemary sprig.

linked-story.headline: High on sobriety

story-elements.text: High on sobriety

Blueberry, Orange Blossom and Vanilla Fizz

This feels almost like a dessert in a glass. Blueberries bring dark-fruit notes, orange blossom water lends a delicate floral aroma, and vanilla rounds out the sharper flavours.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 250 g blueberries, fresh or frozen

— 400 ml chilled water

— 80 ml fresh orange juice

— 40 ml fresh lemon juice

— 60 ml sugar syrup

— 2–4 drops of food-grade orange blossom water

— ¼ tsp vanilla extract

— 400 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— Orange peel twists, for garnish

Method

— Place the blueberries in a saucepan with 100 ml of water. Simmer gently for five minutes, pressing the berries lightly to release their juice.

— Cool the mixture and strain it through a fine sieve, pressing gently to extract the liquid. Allow it to cool completely.

— Combine the blueberry liquid with the remaining water, orange juice, lemon juice and sugar syrup.

— Add the vanilla extract and two drops of orange blossom water. Stir, taste and add another drop or two only if needed.

— Fill four glasses with ice and divide the blueberry mixture equally.

— Top each glass with approximately 100 ml of soda.

— Twist a strip of orange peel over each glass to release its fragrant oils, then use it as a garnish.

Mango, Passion Fruit, Saffron and Lime Cooler

Mango and passion fruit come together for a satisfying contrast: mango provides luscious sweetness, while passion fruit contributes acidity and a distinctive fragrance. Saffron adds subtle floral warmth that makes this drink especially suited to festive occasions.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 300 ml mango pulp or thick mango juice

— 150 ml passion fruit pulp or juice

— 50 ml fresh lime juice

— 1 generous pinch of saffron strands

— 2 tbsp warm water

— 30–45 ml sugar syrup, optional

— 400 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— 4 small mint sprigs, for garnish

— A few passion fruit seeds, for garnish

Method

— Place the saffron strands in two tablespoons of warm water and leave to infuse for 10–15 minutes.

— In a jug, combine the mango pulp, passion fruit pulp and lime juice.

— Add the saffron infusion, including the strands if desired, and mix well.

— Taste before adding sugar syrup. Adjust the consistency with a little water if required.

— Fill four glasses with ice and divide the fruit mixture equally.

— Top each glass with approximately 100 ml of soda, stirring gently to combine.

— Garnish with mint and a few passion fruit seeds.

story-elements.text: Floral cocktails: Bars give traditional flowers a modern twist

Green Apple, Cucumber, Mint and Chilli Refresh

This refreshing combination is ideal for guests who prefer something sharper and less sugary. Green apple gives the drink a tart backbone, cucumber keeps it fresh, mint adds fragrance, and chilli supplies a restrained burst of heat.

Ingredients (serves 4)

— 400 ml green apple juice

— 150 g cucumber, peeled and chopped

— 40 ml fresh lime juice

— 15–20 mint leaves

— 1 small green chilli, deseeded

— 30–45 ml sugar syrup, optional

— 500 ml chilled soda

— 1 cup ice cubes

— 4 cucumber ribbons

— 4 small mint sprigs, for garnish

Method

— Blend the cucumber with 100 ml of the apple juice until smooth.

— Strain through a fine sieve into a jug.

— Add the remaining apple juice, lime juice and mint leaves.

— Slice the deseeded chilli very thinly. Add one or two slices to the jug, stir and taste after two minutes. Remove them once the desired level of heat is achieved.

— Add sugar syrup if needed, especially if the apple juice is particularly tart.

— Divide the mixture between four ice-filled glasses.

— Top each with approximately 125 ml of soda and stir gently.

— Garnish with a cucumber ribbon and a mint sprig.
